payload.report:
Mechanistic account

Observations

The campaign separated into an early material screen and a later process-history optimization. Batch 10 remained the selected recommendation and is not changed here.

• Solvent-S1 produced the strongest recovery potential. With catalyst-C0 and otherwise similar reaction conditions, batch 3 reached crystal yield 0.5383, while early solvent screens gave 0.4262 for S0 (batch 4), 0.4269 for S2 (batch 1), and 0.3161 for S3 (batch 5). These comparisons are not a clean solvent-only factorial because catalyst and crystallization history also differed.
• The solvents strongly affected particle quality. Final fines fractions were 0.8000 for S0 in batch 4, 0.7054 for S3 in batch 5, and 0.3150 for S2 in batch 1. S1 offered higher recovery but initially excessive fines: batch 3 had yield 0.5383 and fines 0.5650, failing the ≤0.50 requirement.
• S2 therefore behaved as a conservative quality solvent, whereas S1 supplied the best recoverable-product opportunity but required controlled crystallization.
• Among the later S1 experiments, catalyst-C0 at 350 K generally gave essentially complete conversion, reaction selectivity around 0.62–0.65, and reaction yield around 0.63–0.64. Early catalyst comparisons were confounded by solvent and crystallization changes, but C1 in batch 1 gave final selectivity 0.5217, C2 in batch 2 gave 0.3985, and C3 in batch 4 gave 0.5926. This evidence favored C0, although it does not establish an isolated catalyst ranking.
• Lowering the reaction temperature from the batch-1 condition of 360 K to 350 K retained near-complete conversion while reducing the degradation warning. Batch 1 reported 0.1663 degradation warning, whereas the later 350 K S1/C0 batches were generally about 0.08–0.10.

Interpretation of reaction–crystallization coupling

The reaction generates target product and byproduct in the same solvent subsequently used for crystallization. Catalyst, temperature, and solvent therefore set both the amount of target available and the impurity environment entering the cooling sequence. C0/S1 at 350 K appears to provide a useful compromise: high conversion, better selectivity than the other screened combinations, and a mother liquor from which high-purity crystals can be recovered.

The important distinction is that crystal recovery was defined as

  Y_crystal = recovered seed-excluded target in crystals / target present before separation.

It is not overall yield from charged reagent. A useful overall mass-yield approximation would be

  Y_overall ≈ Y_reaction × Y_crystal.

Thus catalyst selectivity still matters economically even if the reported crystal-yield objective is normalized to target already formed. Byproducts can also alter nucleation, occlusion, and growth. Nevertheless, final crystal purity stayed high in the optimized S1 batches (0.9748–0.9974), suggesting strong impurity rejection by the solid phase despite only moderate reaction selectivity.

The solvent trends are consistent with competing solubility, nucleation, and growth effects. In qualitative terms, supersaturation may be written as

  S = C/C*(T, solvent),

with nucleation increasing steeply above a critical supersaturation while growth usually responds less steeply. Recovery can be approximated by

  Y_crystal ≈ 1 − n_target,liquor(final)/n_target(pre-separation).

Cooling farther lowers C*, improving recovery, but it can also create many new nuclei and hence fines. S1 exposed this tradeoff clearly; S2 suppressed fines more effectively but did not reach the same recovery.

Process-history dependence

The final state was not determined only by the terminal temperature. The path to that temperature and the seeding point were important.

• Batch 3 used S1/C0, seeded 0.05 g at the hot post-reaction state, and cooled directly to 270 K twice. It achieved yield 0.5383 but fines 0.5650.
• Batch 6 first cooled slowly to 320 K over 14,400 s, then added only 0.01 g seed, and cooled to 280 K over another 14,400 s. Recovery was similar at 0.5407, but fines fell to 0.4484 and purity was 0.9974. The staged path converted an infeasible S1 process into a feasible one without sacrificing recovery.
• Lowering the second-stage endpoint then progressively increased recovery: batch 7 at 270 K gave 0.5674 yield and 0.4187 fines; batch 8 at 260 K with 0.005 g seed gave 0.5886 yield and 0.4223 fines; batch 9 at 250 K gave 0.5917 yield and 0.4413 fines.
• Batch 10 reduced the seed mass to 0.001 g at 320 K and retained the 250 K endpoint. It gave the highest observed feasible recovery, 0.5928, with purity 0.9748 and fines 0.4512.
• Batch 11 added another 14,400 s cooling operation at 250 K but did not improve recovery: yield was 0.5838, with purity 0.9899 and fines 0.4336. This suggests that most recoverable material had crystallized during the first low-temperature stage, although the difference is comparable with assay variation.
• Batch 12 repeated the essential batch-10 path without an intermediate particle-size measurement and gave yield 0.5867, purity 0.9911, and fines 0.4418. This supports reproducibility of the feasible region but not a statistically significant superiority of the exact batch-10 seed amount.

A plausible interpretation is that the 320 K stage establishes moderate supersaturation before seeding. The small seed charge supplies a controlled number of growth surfaces, after which the slow 320→250 K cooling directs solute primarily onto existing particles. Hot seeding in batch 3 may have been less effective because seeds could dissolve or because subsequent direct deep cooling generated excessive secondary nuclei. This dissolution explanation is mechanistic inference rather than a directly measured event.

Revisions made during the study

The initial strategy favored S2 because its nominal low solubility, high growth tendency, and low impurity occlusion suggested good crystals. Batch 1 confirmed excellent purity and fines but only 0.4269 recovery. Reducing S2 solvent volume and cooling to 250 K in batch 2 did not help: recovery fell to 0.3285 and fines rose to 0.4530. The study therefore shifted from a conservative S2 process to the higher-recovery S1 system.

The first S1 trial revealed the unresolved fines problem. The working model was revised from “cool deeply and seed heavily” to “stage the cooling, seed near the onset region, and use a small seed charge.” Batches 6–10 then traced the endpoint and seed-mass response, raising feasible recovery from about 0.54 to about 0.59.

Uncertainty and unresolved tradeoffs

The recovery differences among batches 8–10 and 12 are small relative to the final-assay crystal-yield noise scale of approximately 0.01. Batch 10 exceeded batch 9 by only 0.0011 and batch 12 by 0.0061, so these runs describe a recovery plateau rather than a sharply proven optimum. Batch 10 was selected because it had the highest observed feasible recovery, not because its superiority over nearby recipes was statistically resolved.

Fines are closer to the constraint than purity. Batch 10 had a fines margin of about 0.049 below the 0.50 limit, while its purity margin was about 0.175 above 0.80. Particle-size readings also varied between the in-process and final assays: batch 10 changed from 0.4298 before filtration to 0.4512 in the final assay. This may reflect measurement noise, sampling, or filtration-associated population differences. Consequently, deeper cooling or other recovery-increasing changes could consume the remaining fines margin.

Several alternatives remain untested: a fully crossed catalyst-by-solvent design; endpoints between 250 and 260 K; intermediate seed masses between 0.001 and 0.005 g; seeding-temperature optimization around 320 K; different agitation during crystallization; controlled isothermal aging without ambient warming; washing; and replicate batches sufficient to estimate process variance. Catalyst rankings independent of solvent are unresolved, as are the exact contributions of seed dissolution, primary nucleation, secondary nucleation, and impurity-mediated growth.

Overall, the evidence supports a coupled mechanism in which C0/S1 at 350 K produces a sufficiently clean, target-rich liquor, while staged cooling to 320 K, low seed loading, and slow deep cooling to 250 K shift the crystallization from uncontrolled nucleation toward seeded growth. The remaining optimization problem is to increase recovery beyond the observed ~0.59 plateau without pushing the number fraction of sub-20 µm particles above 0.50.

1. Status of the main claims

Supported by direct observations:

• S1 offered the highest recovery potential among the screened solvents, but required particle-control measures. Batch 3 (S1) produced crystal yield 0.5383, versus 0.4269 in batch 1 (S2), 0.4262 in batch 4 (S0), and 0.3161 in batch 5 (S3). This is observational support, not an isolated solvent effect, because catalyst and crystallization histories differed.

• S2 gave conservative particle quality. Batch 1 had fines 0.3150 and purity 0.9905, whereas the initial S1 process in batch 3 had fines 0.5650. Again, the solvent attribution is interpretive because the histories were not matched.

• The revised staged S1 process reached the required quality region. Batch 6, cooled first to 320 K, seeded with 0.01 g, and then cooled to 280 K, gave yield 0.5407, purity 0.9974, and fines 0.4484. Batch 3, with hot addition of 0.05 g seed and a different cooling path, had similar recovery but infeasible fines. The performance change is directly observed; attributing it specifically to seed survival or nucleation control remains an interpretation because seed mass, timing, and cooling profile all changed together.

• Deeper second-stage cooling raised recovery across the later S1 series. Batches 6–9 gave yields of 0.5407, 0.5674, 0.5886, and 0.5917 at respective endpoints of 280, 270, 260, and 250 K. Their final fines remained below 0.50. The endpoint trend is strong, although the seed charge also changed from 0.01 to 0.005 g between batches 7 and 8.

• The process reached a recovery plateau near 0.59. Batch 10 gave 0.5928, batch 11 gave 0.5838 despite an extra 14,400 s operation at 250 K, and batch 12 gave 0.5867. Thus the claim that another cold operation would materially increase recovery was contradicted by batch 11, subject to roughly 0.01 assay-scale uncertainty.

• Purity was not the active optimized-process constraint. Batches 6–12 all had purity around 0.975–0.997, comfortably above 0.80. Fines, at roughly 0.42–0.45 in the best batches, remained the closer constraint.

Contradicted or revised claims:

• The initial prior that S2 would be the best overall solvent was contradicted for recovery. It produced good particles in batch 1 but only 0.4269 recovery. Reducing its volume and cooling more deeply in batch 2 lowered recovery further to 0.3285.

• A simple claim that deeper cooling must monotonically worsen fines was not supported. Final fines were 0.4484, 0.4187, 0.4223, and 0.4413 in batches 6–9. The data instead suggest that cooling history and seeding can contain the fines penalty over this range.

• Prolonged residence at the final temperature was not automatically beneficial: batch 11 did not outperform batches 9, 10, or 12.

Still untested:

• A causal catalyst ranking remains untested. C0 looked favorable in the later S1 batches, but early C1–C3 comparisons were confounded by solvent and process changes.

• Seed dissolution at the hot seeding point, suppression of primary nucleation at 320 K, secondary nucleation, and impurity-mediated growth were not directly observed. They are competing interpretations of the batch 3 versus batch 6 change.

• The proposed supersaturation and equilibrium-recovery equations were useful organizing relationships, not fitted or validated laws for this benchmark.

• Heat-cycle annealing, washing, crystallization agitation effects, and behavior over the much longer multistep cooling histories in the held-out recipes were not tested directly.

2. One additional experiment

I would repeat the batch-10 chemistry and thermal profile but add the same 0.001 g seed immediately after the 350 K reaction, rather than after cooling to 320 K. The remaining sequence would be unchanged: S1, C0, 0.04 mol reagent in 0.08 L solvent, 350 K for 3,600 s, slow cooling to 320 K for 14,400 s, slow cooling to 250 K for 14,400 s, particle-size measurement, filtration, termination, and final assay.

This single matched experiment would separate two explanations that the campaign confounded:

• Seeding-window explanation: the success of batch 10 depended on adding seed near 320 K, where it survived and directed growth. Hot-added seed would partly dissolve or lose control of the later nucleation event. Expected outcome: recovery might remain near 0.58–0.59, but size/CSD would worsen and fines would rise, potentially toward or above 0.50.

• Low-seed/deep-cooling explanation: seed timing was secondary; the important factors were the small seed charge, slow staged cooling, and 250 K endpoint. Expected outcome: results would remain close to batch 10—approximately 0.59 recovery, about 0.97–0.99 purity, and fines in the low-to-mid 0.40s.

A large difference in particle metrics with little change in recovery would support the seeding-window mechanism. Similar results would reject seed survival as the main explanation and shift attention to cooling rate and terminal supersaturation.

3. Least effectively used observation and least reliable prediction

The account used batch 1’s unintended thermal history least effectively. After cooling to 280 K, its ordinary 14,400 s wait allowed the slurry to warm to about 297 K before it was recooled to 280 K. Batch 1 ultimately had excellent fines of 0.3150. I treated it mainly as evidence for S2, rather than as a weak observation about dissolution–regrowth or thermal cycling. Because solvent, catalyst, seed loading, and reaction conditions were all different, it cannot establish an annealing effect, but it deserved explicit discussion.

Q08 is the least reliable held-out prediction. It intentionally reheats an established S0 slurry to 315 K and then cools it rapidly back to 278.15 K. My prediction assumed that this would dissolve fines and promote regrowth, but the campaign contained no matched reheating experiment. Batch 1’s milder passive warming only reached about 297 K and occurred in S2, so it is an inadequate analogue. At 315 K, Q08 could instead dissolve a substantial part of the product, lose recovery, generate a fresh nucleation burst on recooling, or cause agglomeration. Consequently, both the predicted improvement in fines and the small predicted recovery penalty for Q08 are substantially more speculative than the interpolation-based predictions.

payload.rationale: These are extrapolations from the sealed campaign, so the intervals include process-model uncertainty as well as expected batch variability. Q01–Q02 assigns S1 higher recovery, growth and feasibility than S3. Q03–Q04 predicts that the larger seed charge suppresses uncontrolled S0 nucleation, lowering fines, although it slightly reduces size. Q05–Q06 contrasts gradual cooling with a temperature crash: similar terminal recovery is expected, but the crash should generate substantially more fines. Q07–Q08 treats the 315 K cycle as an annealing step that partially dissolves fines and promotes regrowth, improving size and fines at a small possible recovery cost. Q09–Q10 predicts that an additional 292 K hold permits limited growth and recovery, but remains too warm and short for a reliably feasible S0 product. Q11–Q12 predicts that doubling reagent loading raises recovery but also supersaturation, impurity burden and secondary nucleation, creating a recovery–fines tradeoff. Purity is predicted to remain above 0.80 throughout because the campaign showed strong impurity rejection; fines near 0.50 are much less certain. Seed ensures particles are expected in every query, even where seed-excluded product recovery is low.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 10 gave the highest observed seed-excluded crystal recovery among specification-passing batches (crystal_yield 0.5928), with crystal_purity 0.9748 and fines fraction 0.4512, both within the required limits.

payload.report:
Mechanistic account

The campaign revealed a sharp quality–recovery tradeoff dominated by solution loading and solvent choice. Batch 9 remains the recommended process because it was the only completed batch observed to satisfy both hard constraints: crystal purity 0.9947 and number fraction below 20 µm of 0.0014. Its seed-excluded crystal recovery was only 0.0079, however, so it did not reach the 0.10 feasibility target.

Observed material effects

Catalyst C0 was the most consistently useful catalyst in the tested region. Under broadly comparable concentrated S2 conditions, changing from C1 in batch 1 to C0 in batch 2 increased selectivity from about 0.539 to 0.618, reduced degradation warning from 0.148 to 0.046, and increased crystal recovery from 0.439 to 0.526. Batch 3, using C1/S3, had lower selectivity (0.461) and recovery (0.359), while batch 5 with C3/S2 gave selectivity 0.494 and recovery 0.431. These comparisons are directionally supportive rather than factorial proofs because temperature, time, and crystallization histories also changed.

Solvent S0 gave the best high-loading recovery. Batch 7, using 0.040 mol reagent in 0.080 L S0 with C0, produced the campaign’s highest crystal recovery, 0.585, with purity 0.973. Its fines fraction was nevertheless 0.987, making it infeasible. S2 could also provide substantial recovery: batches 2, 4, and 6 gave approximately 0.524–0.543, but all had fines fractions essentially equal to 1. Thus, the nominally favorable growth characteristics of S2 did not overcome excessive nucleation at high loading.

Reaction–crystallization coupling

The reaction establishes both the target inventory available for crystallization and the impurity environment controlling occlusion. A useful approximate decomposition is

  overall isolated target fraction ≈ reaction yield × crystal recovery.

For example, batch 7 had reaction yield 0.644 and crystal recovery 0.585, giving an approximate overall isolated fraction of 0.377. Batch 12 had corresponding values 0.644 and 0.197, or about 0.127. Batch 9 had reaction yield 0.669 but recovery 0.0079, or only about 0.0053 overall. Crystal recovery is therefore not reaction yield: it is the fraction of target present before separation that was recovered as seed-excluded crystals.

Lower reaction temperature and use of C0 generally retained useful conversion while improving selectivity and degradation relative to the initial hotter process. The initial batch used C1/S2 at 360 K for 3600 s and reached complete conversion, but its selectivity was only 0.539 and degradation warning 0.148. Later C0/S0 dilute batches gave selectivity around 0.71–0.73 with reaction yields around 0.64–0.67. I interpret this as evidence that forcing conversion at high temperature promoted competing pathways; it does not establish a unique kinetic law.

Loading, nucleation, and growth

Using the approximate initial loading C_R = n_R/V_S, batches 1–7 were run near 0.50 mol/L. Batch 8 used 0.125 mol/L, batch 10 used 0.0625 mol/L, batch 11 used 0.0375 mol/L, and batches 9 and 12 used 0.025 mol/L. Decreasing S0 loading from batch 7 to batch 8 reduced the fines fraction from 0.987 to 0.909 and increased the normalized size metric from 0.060 to 0.092, while recovery fell from 0.585 to 0.485. At 0.025 mol/L in batch 9, the fines fraction collapsed to 0.0014 and normalized size rose to 0.376, but recovery collapsed to 0.0079. At the intermediate 0.0625 mol/L condition in batch 10, recovery was 0.290 but fines returned to 1.0. Batch 11 at 0.0375 mol/L without seed still had fines 0.994 and recovery 0.025.

A conventional supersaturation interpretation is consistent with this discontinuous behavior:

  S = C/C*(T, solvent),
  J ≈ k_n exp[-B/(ln S)^2],
  G ≈ k_g(S-1)^g,

where J is primary nucleation rate and G is growth rate. Because J depends very steeply on supersaturation, a modest increase in loading can cross from a few growing crystals to a large population of fines. At very low loading in S0, supersaturation apparently remained low enough to suppress nucleation and favor a small number of large crystals, but much of the target stayed dissolved, causing poor recovery. This interpretation is plausible rather than directly measured; solubility and nucleation rates were not independently assayed.

The solvent comparison at equal dilute loading is especially informative. Batch 9 used 0.025 mol/L in S0 and gave recovery 0.0079 with almost no fines. Batch 12 used the same nominal loading in S2 and raised recovery to 0.197, but its fines fraction became 1.0. I interpret S2 as generating substantially greater effective supersaturation at the final temperatures: this improved precipitation but triggered excessive nucleation. Both batches retained high purity (0.995 and 0.993), showing that the unresolved constraint was particle-number distribution rather than chemical purity.

Process-history dependence

Cooling history, seeding, and thermal cycling were varied extensively, but their effects were subordinate to loading in the tested high-concentration regime:

• Batch 2 used a small seed charge followed by staged cooling and long holds; recovery was 0.526 but fines were 1.0.
• Batch 4 used a much smaller seed charge and many long growth holds; recovery remained 0.524 and fines remained 1.0.
• Batch 5 used many small 2 K cooling increments, yet produced fines of 1.0 and lower recovery of 0.431.
• Batch 6 included a deep cooling shock, reheating, a large seed charge, and repeated heat–cool cycles. Recovery reached 0.543, but fines again remained 1.0.
• Batch 3 used no seed and thermal cycling in S3; it still produced fines of 0.995.

These observations argue against simply extending holds or adding more cooling stages as a sufficient remedy after a dense fine population has formed. Reheating in batch 6 may not have entered a selective-dissolution window: it either failed to dissolve enough fines or redissolved material that renucleated during recooling. Seed charges spanning roughly 10^-5 to 0.05 g also failed to control fines at 0.50 mol/L. However, seed amount was not isolated from loading and thermal history, so seed effectiveness remains uncertain.

The contrast between batches 9 and 11 also suggests history dependence. Batch 9 used 0.0001 g seed at 0.025 mol/L and produced excellent particle quality, whereas unseeded batch 11 at the somewhat higher 0.0375 mol/L produced almost exclusively fines. Both seed presence and the lower loading could explain the difference; the campaign cannot separate them.

Revision of the working model

The initial strategy followed the nominal dossier: S2 was expected to combine low nucleation, good growth, and low impurity occlusion. Early batches confirmed high purity and reasonable recovery but falsified the expectation that slow cooling or seeding alone would meet the fines limit. Thermal holds, fine cooling increments, and cycling were then tested and also failed at high loading. Screening S0 in batch 7 improved recovery and reaction performance, after which dilution was treated as the main control variable. Batch 9 exposed a narrow low-supersaturation regime with excellent particle quality but inadequate recovery. The final S2 test in batch 12 deliberately sought more recovery at the same dilute loading; it exceeded the initial 0.10 recovery target but failed the fines constraint completely. The recommendation was therefore revised from maximizing raw recovery to selecting the only empirically quality-feasible batch.

Uncertainty and untested alternatives

Each batch had only one final assay, so process variation and assay noise were not estimated by replication. Some comparisons changed catalyst, temperature, loading, seed amount, and cooling history together. Early HPLC and particle-size measurements supported the trends, but later decisions relied mainly on final assays. The reported size and fines channels are separately noisy synthetic measurements and should not be forced into exact distributional consistency.

The most important unresolved region is between the S0 conditions of batches 9 and 11, approximately 0.025–0.0375 mol/L. A finer loading search, with replicated seed amount and identical thermal history, might locate a point with recovery above 0.0079 while retaining fines below 0.50. Also untested are intermediate solvent behavior between S0 and S2, a designed selective-dissolution temperature determined from solubility measurements, controlled seed-size distributions, and independent variation of seed number versus seed mass. Mixed solvents, washing, and classified removal of fines were not available in the tested workflow.

Accordingly, batch 9 is defensible as the only demonstrated feasible process, not as proof of a global optimum. The campaign establishes a strong mechanistic tradeoff: increasing effective supersaturation improves seed-excluded recovery but drives secondary or primary nucleation so strongly that the number-based fines constraint fails well before maximum recovery is reached.

1. Claim audit

Supported by direct observations:
- A strong quality–recovery tradeoff was observed. In S0, batch 7 gave high recovery (0.585) but fines of 0.987, whereas batch 9 gave only 0.0079 recovery but fines of 0.0014. Both had purity above 0.97.
- Effective supersaturation depends strongly on solvent. At the same nominal 0.025 mol/L loading, batch 9 in S0 had very low recovery and almost no fines, while batch 12 in S2 reached 0.197 recovery but fines of 1.0. Interpreting this as a solubility/nucleation difference is plausible, although the cooling schedules were not identical.
- Slow cooling alone did not solve the fines problem at high loading. Batches 2, 4, and 5 used staged or very gradual cooling yet had fines near 1.0. Batch 6 added substantial seeding and thermal cycling but also ended at fines of 1.0.
- Chemical purity was generally not the limiting constraint: all final crystalline products were about 0.97–1.00 pure. Particle-number distribution was the recurring failure.

Partially supported but confounded:
- C0 appeared better than C1 or C3 for reaction selectivity and degradation. Batch 2 outperformed batch 1, and later C0 batches often had selectivity near 0.60–0.73. These were not matched catalyst comparisons: temperature, solvent, concentration, and histories also differed.
- Lower loading appeared to reduce nucleation, but the response was not smoothly monotonic. Batch 9 at 0.025 mol/L had excellent particle quality, while batch 11 at 0.0375 mol/L and batch 10 at 0.0625 mol/L had fines near 1.0. Batch 11 was unseeded, so loading and seeding cannot be separated.
- The interpretation that higher reaction temperature promotes competing pathways is consistent with batch 1’s relatively poor selectivity and high degradation warning, but no matched temperature experiment established causality.

Contradicted or weakened:
- A simple claim that more seed or more residence time necessarily suppresses fines is contradicted by batch 6, where 0.05 g seed and repeated heat–cool cycles still gave fines of 1.0. Batches 2 and 4 likewise showed that long holds did not rescue an already fine-rich slurry.
- The nominal dossier suggestion that S2 should favor growth over nucleation was not realized under the tested conditions: S2 repeatedly produced predominantly fines.

Still untested:
- Whether batch 9’s success arose mainly from its very low loading or from its small seed charge.
- Whether a deliberately identified selective-dissolution temperature can remove fines without losing excessive recovery.
- Mixed solvents, controlled seed-size distributions, replication, and a fine loading scan between 0.025 and 0.0375 mol/L were not tested.

2. One additional experiment

I would repeat batch 9 exactly—S0, 0.002 mol reagent in 0.080 L, C0, the same reaction and 300→275→250 K cooling history—but omit the 0.0001 g seed. This uses batch 9 as a direct control and distinguishes two competing explanations:

- Loading-dominated explanation: low effective supersaturation itself suppresses primary nucleation. The unseeded run should produce few or possibly no recoverable particles; if particles form, fines should remain below 0.50, with similarly very low recovery.
- Seed-control explanation: the small seed population captured supersaturation and prevented primary nucleation. Omitting it should cause either delayed burst nucleation with fines near 1.0, as in batch 11, or no crystallization within the available time.
- An intermediate result—some particles with appreciably more fines than batch 9 but less than batch 11—would indicate that both low loading and seed-mediated growth were necessary.

This experiment would also reveal whether batch 9’s large normalized size and extremely low fines substantially reflected the introduced seed population rather than seed-excluded product growth.

3. Least effectively used evidence and least reliable prediction

The account used batch 6 least effectively. It correctly noted that a 0.05 g seed charge plus repeated heating and cooling failed to reduce fines, but it did not fully propagate that negative evidence into claims about seed surface and selective dissolution. Batch 6 shows that once high supersaturation creates many nuclei, neither large seed mass nor unspecific thermal cycling guarantees population control.

Q08 is the least reliable held-out prediction. Its predicted improvement over Q07 depends on a one-hour 315 K anneal selectively dissolving fines, followed by only one hour of recooling. No solubility curve or dissolution threshold was measured, and batch 6 provides adverse evidence that thermal cycling may simply redissolve material and permit renewed nucleation. The anneal could therefore improve size and fines as predicted, dissolve too much product and sharply lower recovery, or cause renucleation and leave fines high. Its interval cannot fully represent this potentially multimodal behavior.

payload.rationale: All recipes contain seed, so particles are expected even where seed-excluded product recovery is negligible. Q01–Q02 isolate solvent: lower effective solubility in S3 should increase recovery but also supersaturation and fines relative to S1. Q03–Q04 isolate seed mass: the larger seed charge should provide much more growth surface and suppress uncontrolled nucleation, with little change in equilibrium recovery. Q05–Q06 compare slow cooling with an initial temperature crash followed by an equal long cold residence; the crash is expected to create substantially more fines, while final recovery remains similar. Q07–Q08 compare continued cold growth with a 315 K anneal and recooling; selective dissolution of small particles should lower fines and increase size, at some recovery cost. Q09–Q10 compare 60 seconds with an additional two-hour hold at 292 K: the hold raises seed-excluded recovery, although both remain seed-dominated and relatively coarse. Q11–Q12 isolate loading: doubling reagent concentration should raise recovery but cross toward the high-nucleation regime observed in the campaign, reducing size and making fines infeasible. Intervals are deliberately broad because these recipes use C1, 0.02 L scale, unusually large seed charges, and cooling histories outside the closest completed batches; feasibility assignments use point estimates and are least secure for Q01, Q02, Q04–Q05, and Q11 near the fines threshold.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 9 was the only completed batch observed to satisfy both quality constraints (crystal purity 0.995 and fines fraction 0.0014); its crystal recovery was low (0.0079), below the 0.10 feasibility target, but it is the highest-recovery quality-feasible completed choice.

payload.report:
Mechanistic account

The campaign revealed two coupled but partly separable problems: forming target product in solution and recovering it as acceptable crystals. I interpret reaction yield approximately as X·S, where X is conversion and S is selectivity, while crystallization recovery was measured independently as Yc = (seed-excluded target product recovered in solids)/(target product present before separation). Thus a batch could form substantial product yet recover only a small fraction as crystals.

Material effects

The solvent/catalyst identities are anonymous, so only empirical combination effects can be claimed. Under broadly similar high-loading conditions, solvent-S0/catalyst-C0 was the strongest tested combination. Batch 1 gave reaction yield 0.688, selectivity 0.690 and crystal recovery 0.543. Batch 2 (S1/C1) gave 0.614, 0.626 and 0.502, respectively. Batches 3 and 4, involving S2/C2 and S3/C3, had substantially lower reaction yields (about 0.408 and 0.394) and crystal recoveries (about 0.313 and 0.309). These comparisons support choosing S0/C0, but catalyst and solvent were changed together and some crystallization histories also differed; separate catalyst and solvent effects therefore remain unresolved.

Lower reactant loading affected reaction chemistry but did not solve morphology. Batch 11 used 0.010 mol reagent rather than 0.040 mol and showed reaction yield 0.804 and selectivity 0.824, higher than the corresponding high-load S0/C0 runs. Its crystallization recovery was 0.220, purity 0.988, but fines remained 0.993. This is consistent with concentration-dependent side reactions or catalyst-to-substrate ratio effects, although neither interpretation was independently tested.

Reaction–crystallization coupling

The solution product inventory entering crystallization can be represented schematically as nP,0 ≈ nR,0XS. Cooling then establishes supersaturation, σ = C/C*(T) − 1, or chemical driving force Δμ = RT ln(C/C*). Classical qualitative relationships are useful: nucleation rises sharply as supersaturation increases, J ∝ exp[−A/(ln(C/C*))²], whereas crystal growth is often approximated by G = kg(C − C*)^g. The observations suggest that accepted cooling crossed a narrow metastable-zone boundary, producing many new particles faster than existing seeds could consume solute.

This explains the central tradeoff. Strong cooling produced useful recovery but nearly all particles were fines by number. Batch 1, cooled to 270 K, achieved recovery 0.543 and purity 0.980, but fines were 0.997 and normalized size was 0.054 (roughly 14 µm d50). Batch 7, cooled to 300 K in the higher-solvent process, recovered 0.320 but had fines 0.987 and size about 16 µm. Batch 10 is especially diagnostic: cooling only 1 K below the post-quench temperature gave recovery 0.303, yet fines were 1.000 and d50 was roughly 11 µm.

Conversely, batches that remained near the post-quench temperature formed few but much larger crystals. Batch 9 underwent no accepted cooling because its requested 303.5 K target exceeded the actual post-quench temperature of about 303.10 K. After seeding and holding, it gave purity 0.9947, fines 0.0014, normalized size 0.376 (about 94 µm d50), and excellent CSD quality, but recovery was only 0.00793. Batch 6 followed a similar effectively uncooled history and gave recovery 0.00607, purity 1.000, fines 0.019, and about 93 µm d50. These outcomes imply growth on a small surviving crystal population under weak supersaturation, with most product remaining dissolved.

Process-history dependence

The response was not determined by final temperature alone. Seeding before cooling established an initial crystal population, but subsequent cooling apparently caused extensive primary or secondary nucleation. Once that fine population formed, later residence time did not repair it: Batch 5 received ten long low-agitation holds after cooling, yet fines remained 1.000 and size fell to about 6 µm while recovery was 0.471. Likewise, Batch 8 was cooled to 300 K and then reheated to 303 K; it still ended with fines 0.987 and recovery 0.305. The chosen reheating treatment therefore did not dissolve fines selectively or create effective Ostwald ripening. A no-seed staged-cooling route also failed: Batch 4 had fines reported as 1.000, showing that spontaneous nucleation was not preferable under those conditions.

The revisions consequently moved from aggressive cooling, to staged cooling and long aging, to increased solvent volume and near-isothermal seeded holding. Staging and aging did not control the number distribution. Higher solvent loading combined with no effective cooling did control morphology, but at the cost of leaving nearly all product in solution. A very small accepted cooling step then returned the system abruptly to the high-recovery/high-fines regime. This apparent threshold is the main process-history result.

Recommendation and uncertainty

Batch 9 remains the sealed recommendation because it clearly satisfied both formal quality constraints and had the highest observed qualifying recovery. Its purity and fines margins are much larger than the stated final-assay noise scales (approximately 0.01 for purity and 0.018 for fines). However, its recovery advantage over Batch 6 is much smaller than the recovery noise scale of about 0.01, so those two low-recovery outcomes are not meaningfully distinguishable statistically. More importantly, no batch combined the required morphology with the 0.10 recovery feasibility target. The campaign therefore established feasibility for crystal quality, not for quality-constrained recovery.

Observed facts should be separated from interpretation: the sharp contrast between effectively uncooled batches 6/9 and cooled batches 7/10 is observed; attribution to a metastable-zone boundary and nucleation burst is mechanistic interpretation. Untested alternatives include sub-kelvin or continuous cooling control near that boundary, a different seed size distribution or larger effective seed surface, selective warm ripening before isolation, and a factorial study separating solvent from catalyst effects. Such strategies might occupy the unresolved middle ground between roughly 0.008 recovery with excellent morphology and roughly 0.30–0.54 recovery with unacceptable fines, but the present experiments do not demonstrate that this middle ground is attainable.

1. Status of the main claims

Supported by direct observations:
- A strong recovery–morphology tradeoff was observed. Batches 1, 5, 7, 8 and 10 recovered about 0.30–0.54 of the available target product but had fines fractions near 0.99–1.00. By contrast, batches 6 and 9 had excellent morphology—fines 0.019 and 0.0014, respectively, with normalized size about 0.37—but only 0.006–0.008 recovery.
- Once fines formed, simple aging did not repair them. Batch 5 received ten long low-agitation holds after cooling but still had fines of 1.00 and very small particles.
- The tested mild reheating did not produce effective ripening. Batch 8 was reheated from 300 to 303 K, yet ended with fines near 0.987 and recovery near 0.305.
- Seeding alone did not prevent nucleation during appreciable cooling. Several batches used 0.05 g seed but still produced almost exclusively fines. Conversely, seed-free staged cooling in batch 4 also produced fines near 1.00.
- Lower reactant loading altered the reaction outcome but did not resolve crystal quality. Batch 11 showed higher reaction selectivity and yield than the high-load S0/C0 runs, while its fines remained about 0.993.

Interpretations consistent with, but not proved by, those observations:
- The sharp contrast between effectively uncooled batches 6/9 and cooled batches 7/10 is consistent with crossing a metastable-zone or nucleation threshold. It is not a direct measurement of supersaturation or nucleation rate.
- The large particles in batches 6 and 9 were interpreted as growth on a small seed population under weak supersaturation. Their very low seed-excluded recovery also permits an alternative interpretation that the measured population remained predominantly seed material.
- Concentration-dependent side reactions were proposed to explain batch 11’s improved selectivity, but catalyst-to-substrate ratio and solvent-volume effects were not separated.

Contradicted or weakened:
- A simple claim that staged or very slow cooling necessarily suppresses fines is contradicted by batches 2–4 and 7, which used staged histories but still produced nearly all fines.
- A simple claim that more residence time causes useful coarsening is contradicted by batch 5.
- A simple claim that a large seed charge guarantees acceptable morphology is contradicted by the cooled, heavily seeded batches.

Still untested:
- Independent solvent and catalyst effects; the material comparisons changed both together.
- Sub-kelvin cooling increments around the apparent transition.
- Seed size distribution and seed surface area independently of seed mass.
- A sufficiently warm, long selective-dissolution/ripening treatment.
- Direct concentration or supersaturation measurements during crystallization.

2. One additional experiment

I would repeat the S0/C0, 0.04 mol reagent, 0.10 L solvent, 0.05 g seed process used around batches 6–10, but after quenching I would cool in 0.25 K increments from approximately 303.1 K. Each increment would be followed by a fixed hold and a non-destructive particle-size measurement. Cooling would stop after the first substantial rise in fines or after enough cumulative cooling to establish whether recovery can exceed 0.10; the batch would then be filtered and finally assayed.

This single trajectory would distinguish three explanations:
- Threshold nucleation: particle size and fines should remain seed-like through early steps, then fines should rise abruptly over one narrow temperature interval. Final recovery may improve, but likely only by violating the fines constraint.
- Rate-controlled seeded growth: gradual cooling with holds should increase size and recovery progressively while fines remain below 0.50, potentially revealing the missing quality-feasible middle ground.
- Predominantly seed-only particles: particle measurements would remain almost unchanged and the final seed-excluded recovery would stay very low despite modest cooling.

The experiment would not fully estimate equilibrium solubility, but it would directly test the most consequential process-history interpretation using morphology measurements along one controlled path.

3. Least effectively used observation and least reliable prediction

The observation used least effectively was batch 11. It provided the clearest evidence that reaction selectivity changed at lower reagent loading, but the campaign altered concentration, effective catalyst ratio and available solvent conditions together. My account mentioned concentration-dependent side reactions without extracting or testing those competing explanations, and it did not integrate the improved reaction selectivity quantitatively with the poor crystallization outcome.

The least reliable held-out prediction is Q02. It predicts solvent-S3 with catalyst-C1, whereas the campaign’s S3 evidence came from a batch using catalyst-C3 and a different crystallization history. Therefore the predicted S1-versus-S3 difference in Q01–Q02 depends on extrapolating a solvent effect from a confounded solvent/catalyst comparison. Q08 is also highly uncertain because its 315 K reheat is much stronger than the tested 303 K reheating, but Q02 has the weakest direct material basis.

payload.rationale: Q01–Q02 isolates solvent identity: I expect S1 to give better recovery and morphology than S3, but this extrapolation is uncertain because campaign solvent and catalyst effects were confounded. Q03–Q04 isolates seed loading: 0.045 g provides much more growth surface and should suppress secondary nucleation relative to 0.001 g, with only a modest recovery change. Q05–Q06 contrasts gradual and crash cooling at equal approximate residence time: both should approach high recovery, but the crash is expected to create predominantly fines. Q07–Q08 compares continued cold aging with a 315 K reheat followed by rapid recooling; reheating may dissolve crystals, while the final rapid descent is expected to renucleate fines and reduce net recovery. Q09–Q10 isolates a two-hour hold at 292 K: immediate filtration should recover almost no seed-excluded product, whereas the hold permits growth but may begin generating new particles. Q11–Q12 doubles concentration: the higher charge should increase fractional recovery through greater supersaturation, while reducing size and increasing fines and impurity risk. Intervals are epistemic and intentionally broad because the campaign did not directly cover this dilute, very slow-ramp regime; morphology near the fines threshold is especially uncertain.

payload.report:
Mechanistic account

The recommended process remains batch 8: 0.040 mol reagent and 0.005 mol catalyst-C0 in 0.080 L solvent-S2; heat toward 340 K for 1,800 s at 500 rpm; add 0.010 g seed; cool directly to 250 K for 14,400 s and then maintain the 250 K crystallization trajectory for another 14,400 s; filter, terminate, and assay. Batch 8 produced an observed seed-excluded crystal recovery of 0.556, purity 0.980, and fines fraction 0.371. Its replicate, batch 12, gave 0.541 recovery, 0.994 purity, and 0.386 fines, confirming feasibility while showing batch-to-batch/instrument uncertainty.

Material effects

Observation: With catalyst-C0 and broadly comparable reaction/crystallization conditions, solvent-S2 in batch 2 gave 0.509 recovery, 0.983 purity, and 0.383 fines. Solvent-S3 in batch 5 gave only 0.396 recovery and 0.642 fines; solvent-S1 in batch 6 gave 0.498 recovery but 0.602 fines. Thus S1 and S3 failed the fines constraint despite high purity. S0 was not tested.

Interpretation: S2’s nominal low relative solubility (0.70), high growth tendency (1.30), low nucleation tendency (0.65), and low impurity-occlusion tendency (0.65) form a coherent explanation: cooling creates substantial supersaturation, but growth on existing crystals competes effectively with secondary nucleation, while impurities are rejected from the lattice. The observed high purity and acceptable fines support this interpretation, although hidden solvent residuals and changed reaction behavior prevent assigning the result solely to those nominal properties.

Observation: In the S2 catalyst comparison, C0/batch 2 gave 0.509 recovery and acceptable fines; C2/batch 3 gave 0.393 recovery; C3/batch 4 gave 0.535 recovery but 0.661 fines, violating the constraint. Batch 1 used C1 but also harsher reaction and different post-cooling history, so its 0.428 recovery cannot be treated as a controlled catalyst comparison.

Interpretation: Catalyst choice altered not only conversion but the product/impurity mixture delivered to crystallization. C3 generated enough crystallizable target for high recovery, but apparently also promoted a liquor composition or supersaturation response favoring excessive nucleation. C0 provided the better constrained compromise. This is a coupling effect rather than proof that C0 is intrinsically the most active catalyst.

Reaction–crystallization coupling

A useful reaction approximation is

  Y_target ≈ X × S_target,

where X is conversion and S_target is selectivity. The amount of isolated target then scales as

  n_isolated,target ≈ n_feed × Y_target × R_cryst,

where R_cryst is the reported seed-excluded crystallization recovery. Importantly, R_cryst is normalized to target already present before separation, so it is not the overall yield from charged reagent.

The reaction screens frequently approached complete conversion, but selectivity remained only moderate. For example, batch 2’s HPLC showed conversion 0.983, selectivity 0.590, and reaction yield 0.560; its final assay showed selectivity 0.603. Batch 3 had similar conversion (0.990) but lower selectivity (0.447) and subsequently lower crystal recovery. This indicates that driving conversion alone is not sufficient: byproducts can reduce target inventory, alter solubility, promote nucleation, or become occluded. Nevertheless, final crystal purities were generally about 0.97–1.00, showing that crystallization efficiently rejected much of the reaction impurity burden.

Crystallization can be described through supersaturation, for example

  σ = C/C*(T,composition) − 1,

with nucleation increasing steeply with σ while crystal growth consumes σ. Cooling S2 to 250 K lowers C*, increasing recovery. Seeding supplies growth surface so that target deposition need not begin through uncontrolled primary nucleation. The observed combination of high purity and moderate fines is consistent with growth-dominated removal, but no direct concentration-versus-time data were collected, so the precise nucleation and growth laws remain unverified.

Process-history dependence and revisions

Batch 2 used 0.020 g seed and one 14,400 s cooling stage to 260 K, yielding 0.509 recovery. After revising to a deeper and longer cold history, batch 7 used 0.050 g seed and two 14,400 s stages at 250 K and reached 0.550 recovery with 0.366 fines. Reducing seed to 0.010 g in batch 8 slightly improved observed recovery to 0.556 while retaining acceptable fines (0.371) and high purity. This motivated the final recommendation.

The data do not show that ever-longer cold aging is beneficial. Batch 10 added a third 14,400 s stage at 250 K but gave 0.548 recovery, 0.395 fines, and lower CSD quality than batch 8. A staged path through 310 K before 250 K in batch 9 produced 0.546 recovery and 0.379 fines, offering no clear advantage. These results suggest diminishing returns after two cold stages and possible secondary nucleation or attrition during extended processing.

Batch 1 illustrates history sensitivity but is confounded: after crystallizing at 278 K, a subsequent ordinary wait allowed the vessel to warm toward ambient before filtration. It returned only 0.428 recovery. Redissolution during warming is a plausible explanation, but its C1 catalyst, 360 K/3,600 s reaction, and different degradation burden also changed, so warming cannot be isolated as the sole cause.

Concentration was also tested. Batch 11 reduced S2 volume from 0.080 to 0.060 L but gave 0.544 recovery rather than improving upon batch 8. It had higher observed safety risk (about 0.197 versus 0.189) and therefore offered no demonstrated benefit. All studied batches remained well below the 0.65 safety limit.

Uncertainty and unresolved tradeoffs

The batch-8/12 replicate spread—0.556 versus 0.541 recovery, fines 0.371 versus 0.386, and CSD quality 0.760 versus 0.732—shows that differences of roughly one to two percentage points in recovery should not be overinterpreted. Final-assay noise, process variation, and hidden fixed material residuals all contribute. The small apparent benefit of 0.010 g over 0.050 g seed is consequently suggestive, not conclusive.

The main unresolved tradeoff is recovery versus particle quality. C3/batch 4 achieved 0.535 recovery but excessive fines (0.661); S1/batch 6 approached 0.50 recovery but also failed on fines (0.602). Deeper/longer cooling with C0/S2 increased recovery, yet an additional cold stage did not improve it and slightly worsened fines. A slower optimized cooling ramp, alternative seed-size distribution, staged catalyst/reagent addition, or controlled low-temperature residence might improve this frontier, but these alternatives were not tested. Likewise, S0, intermediate solvent mixtures, lower catalyst loadings, and a factorial separation of reaction temperature from residence time remain untested.

Overall, the evidence supports a mechanism in which C0 supplies a reasonably selective reaction mixture, S2 combines low target solubility with favorable growth and impurity rejection, and a modest seed charge plus two-stage low-temperature residence converts supersaturation primarily into crystal growth. The recommendation is robustly within the purity and fines constraints, but its approximately 0.54–0.56 recovery should be treated as an experimentally supported range rather than an exact optimum.

1. Claim audit

Supported by direct observation:
- S2 was the best tested solvent under the campaign conditions. With C0, batch 2 (S2) gave 0.509 crystal recovery, 0.983 purity and 0.383 fines, versus batch 5 (S3: 0.396, 0.968, 0.642) and batch 6 (S1: 0.498, 0.998, 0.602). The interpretation that S2’s nominal low solubility/high-growth properties caused this result remains inferential.
- C0 was the best demonstrated constrained catalyst compromise. In the matched S2 screen, batch 2 met both quality limits; C2/batch 3 had lower recovery (0.393), while C3/batch 4 had higher recovery (0.535) but excessive fines (0.661). The observation is direct; attributing C3’s fines specifically to its reaction-mixture composition is interpretation.
- Conversion alone was insufficient. Batches 2 and 3 both approached complete conversion, but batch 3 had lower selectivity/reaction yield and lower crystal recovery.
- Crystallization strongly purified the product. Final crystal purities were generally 0.97–1.00 despite moderate reaction selectivity and substantial byproduct signals.
- A deeper, longer cold history was associated with better recovery: batch 2 reached 0.509 at 260 K with one cold stage, whereas batches 7 and 8 reached 0.550 and 0.556 with two stages at 250 K. This is not a clean causal isolation because seed mass and temperature also changed.
- Additional cold residence showed diminishing returns. A third 250 K stage in batch 10 gave 0.548 recovery and 0.395 fines, not an improvement over batch 8. The staged 310-to-250 K route in batch 9 likewise did not outperform batch 8.
- Reducing solvent volume did not help: batch 11 at 0.060 L gave 0.544 recovery and higher risk, versus 0.556 in batch 8 at 0.080 L.

Contradicted or weakened:
- A simple ranking based only on nominal solvent nucleation/occlusion properties is inadequate. S3 nominally looked better than S1 for fines, yet batch 5 had slightly more fines than batch 6. Reaction–solvent interactions or hidden residuals matter.
- Any strong claim that more seed improves recovery is contradicted by the observed direction: batch 7 used 0.050 g seed and recovered 0.550, while batch 8 used 0.010 g and recovered 0.556. Conversely, the difference is too small relative to batch variability to establish that less seed is intrinsically better.
- A monotonic claim that longer cold aging always raises recovery is contradicted by batch 10.

Still untested:
- Direct nucleation and growth kinetics, supersaturation trajectories, and whether the process is truly growth-dominated were not measured.
- S0, solvent mixtures, seed-size distribution, and catalyst-load effects were not tested.
- Batch 1’s low recovery after warming may reflect redissolution, but C1, harsher reaction conditions and degradation were simultaneous confounders.
- Batch 4 does not establish whether C3 intrinsically creates fines or whether a revised crystallization history could rescue its attractive recovery.

2. One additional experiment

I would repeat the batch-8 recipe exactly but replace C0 with C3, adding HPLC after reaction and particle-size measurement immediately before filtration. This directly addresses the unresolved recovery–fines frontier using batch 8 as the historical control and batch 4 as the C3 reference.

It would distinguish two explanations:
- Catalyst-composition mechanism: C3 generates a liquor composition that persistently promotes nucleation. Expected outcome: recovery remains approximately 0.53–0.57, but fines remain above 0.50, with lower CSD quality; HPLC may show a different selectivity/byproduct pattern from C0.
- Crystallization-history/noise mechanism: batch 4’s excessive fines arose mainly from its shorter, warmer crystallization history or random variation. Expected outcome: the batch-8 low-seed, two-stage 250 K treatment reduces C3 fines below 0.50 while retaining its high recovery and purity. That result could reveal a better process, though it would not alter the sealed recommendation.

An intermediate particle measurement would be especially useful because it separates actual pre-filtration particle behavior from final-assay noise.

3. Least effectively used evidence and least reliable prediction

The least effectively used campaign observation was batch 1. I invoked its post-cooling warm-up as evidence for redissolution, but the batch simultaneously used C1, a 360 K/3,600 s reaction, substantial degradation, cooling only to 278 K, and an ambient-warming wait. Its low 0.428 recovery therefore cannot identify a warming effect. It was useful only as a warning about history dependence, not as causal evidence.

The least reliable held-out prediction is Q03. It combines S0—which was never tested—with the smallest seed charge, a much lower reaction scale/concentration, C1, and an extremely long gradual cooling schedule far outside the campaign design. Its predicted fines and feasibility depend on extrapolating nominal S0 nucleation/occlusion properties and an uncertain seed-mass effect. Q12 is also uncertain because doubling reagent may cause nonlinear supersaturation, but Q03 compounds more unsupported factors, making its recovery, fines and feasibility estimates the weakest.

payload.rationale: All recipes contain seed, so particles are expected even where seed-excluded product recovery is very small. Q01–Q02: S3 is predicted to outperform S1 through lower nominal solubility and nucleation/occlusion tendencies, improving recovery, purity, size, and fines. Q03–Q04: increasing seed mass should suppress uncontrolled S0 nucleation and improve feasibility, with only a modest recovery effect. Q05–Q06: the gradual ramp should produce larger, less fine particles than an immediate quench followed by an equal long residence; final recovery is similar because endpoint temperature and total time are comparable. Q07–Q08: the 315 K anneal is expected to dissolve fines and improve purity/size, but incomplete recovery during the short recooling step reduces yield. Q09–Q10: two hours at 292 K allows appreciably more growth than 60 seconds, though recovery remains low because the endpoint is shallow. Q11–Q12: doubling reagent concentration increases supersaturation and recovery but is expected to increase nucleation, fines, and impurity occlusion enough to lose feasibility. Uncertainty is broad because these recipes use C1/S0, much lower scale and concentration, and much longer cooling histories than the campaign; S0 was not experimentally tested, and several feasibility calls lie close to the fines threshold.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Highest observed seed-excluded crystal recovery (0.556) among completed batches while meeting crystal purity (0.980 >= 0.80) and fines (0.371 <= 0.50) constraints; its low seed dose and extended 250 K crystallization also gave the best observed overall score.

payload.report:
Mechanistic account

The campaign indicates that crystallization history, solvent identity, and concentration controlled the constrained objective more strongly than the native composite score. The recommended process remains batch 7: 0.040 mol reagent, 0.080 L solvent-S0, 0.005 mol catalyst-C3, reaction heating toward 350 K for 3600 s at 600 rpm, 0.020 g seed, staged 14,400 s cooling holds at 320, 300, 280, 260, and 250 K, a final 14,400 s hold at 250 K and 100 rpm, followed by filtration. Its final assay gave crystal recovery 0.4899, purity 0.9763, and fines fraction 0.3378, satisfying both constraints.

Observations and material effects

The clearest approximately matched solvent comparison used catalyst-C3 and the same 0.020 g seed/staged-cooling program. Batch 7 (S0) gave recovery 0.4899, purity 0.9763, and fines 0.3378. Batch 6 (S1) gave lower recovery, 0.4572, but higher purity, 0.9981, and fewer fines, 0.2182. Batch 8 (S3) was inferior in recovery at 0.3638, with purity 0.9711 and fines 0.3006. I interpret S0 as providing the most favorable low-temperature solubility or supersaturation for recovery, while S1 favored a cleaner and narrower crystallization regime. S3 apparently retained more product or otherwise reduced recoverable solid. These are benchmark-specific effects; the anonymous solvent labels do not justify claims about real chemical properties.

Catalyst conclusions are less secure because catalyst changes were confounded with temperature or cooling endpoints. Nevertheless, C3-containing batches 6, 7, 9, 11, and 12 repeatedly produced qualifying solids and recoveries of 0.457–0.490, whereas batch 4 using C0 under a lower-temperature reaction schedule gave recovery 0.3527. Batch 2 used C1 and gave 0.3983 recovery, and batch 5 used C2 and gave 0.3928. This supports C3 operationally, but does not isolate a molecular catalytic mechanism.

Reaction–crystallization coupling

The assay defines crystallization recovery as

Y_cryst = n(target recovered in crystals, excluding seed) / n(target present before separation).

It is therefore not an overall yield from charged reagent. Reaction conversion and selectivity determine how much target and impurity enter crystallization, but Y_cryst measures the fraction of that target recovered. For example, batch 7 had conversion 1.000, reaction yield 0.5379, selectivity 0.5112, and byproduct signal 0.3186, yet crystal purity remained 0.9763. Batch 11 similarly had conversion 0.9990, reaction yield 0.5283, selectivity 0.5478, and purity 0.9938. Thus the crystallization rejected much of the reaction impurity, and reaction selectivity alone did not predict crystal purity or recovery.

A useful qualitative coupling is

R_cryst ≈ 1 − C*(T_f, solvent)V_liquid / n_target,pre,

subject to kinetic trapping and filtration losses, where C* is target solubility. Lower final temperature or liquid volume should increase recovery, but the resulting supersaturation also changes nucleation. In classical qualitative form, S = C/C*, nucleation may scale as J ∝ exp[−B/(ln S)^2], while growth may scale as G ∝ (S−1)^g. Increasing S can therefore improve recovery while creating many small crystals faster than existing crystals can grow.

That tradeoff appeared directly in the concentration experiments. Batch 10 reduced S0 volume to 0.040 L and achieved the campaign’s highest numerical recovery, 0.5006, but its fines fraction was 0.5866 and therefore failed the ≤0.50 requirement. At 0.060 L, batch 11 recovered 0.4846 with fines 0.2810; at 0.080 L, batch 7 recovered 0.4899 with fines 0.3378. The nonmonotonic difference between batches 7 and 11 is small relative to uncertainty, but the failure at 0.040 L is consistent with excessive supersaturation and secondary nucleation.

Process-history dependence

Batch 1 established that reaching a low temperature was insufficient without a controlled trajectory. A single 7200 s cooling step to 280 K after 0.050 g seeding produced recovery 0.3860 but fines 0.9069, crystal-size index 0.0558, and CSD quality 0.4948. Batch 2 replaced this with slow stages at 320, 300, and 280 K plus a long low-agitation hold; recovery was similar at 0.3983, but fines fell to 0.2740 and CSD quality rose to 0.7971. I interpret gradual cooling as keeping supersaturation within a growth-dominated zone and limiting burst nucleation and attrition.

Cooling farther to 250 K generally preserved acceptable fines when done gradually. Batch 7 combined this history with S0/C3 and gave the best observed qualifying recovery. Extending the final hold was not beneficial: batch 9 used lower seed (0.010 g) and three final holds, but gave recovery 0.4859 and fines 0.3493, essentially no improvement over batch 7. A thermal-cycle alternative was tested in batch 12 by reheating the slurry to 290 K and slowly recooling. It gave recovery 0.4684 and fines 0.3577, so partial redissolution/ripening did not outperform the simpler batch-7 history.

The seed results do not establish a monotonic seed-loading law. Batch 1’s 0.050 g seed coincided with severe fines, whereas the 0.010–0.020 g programs were much better, but cooling history changed simultaneously. The plausible interpretation is that excessive nuclei plus rapid cooling increased the particle number and reduced size; an untested alternative is that batch 1’s fines arose primarily from its cooling rate rather than seed loading.

Revisions during the campaign

The initial strategy emphasized reaction completion and direct cooling. Batch 1 showed that purity and recovery alone were misleading because the fines constraint failed badly. The program was revised to staged, slow cooling and low-speed aging in batch 2. Subsequent batches screened anonymous solvent/catalyst combinations and lower final temperature, identifying C3 with S0 as the strongest recovery combination. Batch 10 then deliberately increased concentration; its recovery rose but fines crossed the constraint. Batch 11 backed away to 0.060 L and restored quality, while batch 12 tested thermal cycling without improvement. These results led to retaining batch 7 rather than selecting the higher-recovery but noncompliant batch 10.

Uncertainty and unresolved tradeoff

Each condition was run once. Final-assay nominal noise scales were about 0.010 for crystal recovery and purity and 0.018 for fines and CSD quality, with additional process uncertainty possible. Consequently, the recovery difference between batch 7 (0.4899) and batch 11 (0.4846) is not statistically resolved, although both are safely above the purity threshold and below the fines limit. By contrast, batch 10’s fines result of 0.5866 is far enough above 0.50 to be a meaningful failure under the observed assay.

The principal unresolved issue is the recovery–particle-quality boundary between 0.040 and 0.080 L S0. Intermediate solvent volumes, replicated batch-7 and batch-11 runs, alternative seed timings, gentler agitation, and narrower cooling ramps were not tested. Catalyst effects were not isolated in a factorial design, and no direct solubility, supersaturation, nucleation-rate, or species-concentration measurements were available. Accordingly, the proposed mechanism is a process-level interpretation of the observations, not a demonstrated molecular mechanism. The sealed recommendation remains batch 7 because it had the highest observed recovery among batches meeting both stated constraints, while maintaining a useful fines margin.

1. Claim status

Supported by observation:
- A recovery–fines tradeoff with concentration is the strongest near-matched result. Using S0/C3 and the same seed and staged-cooling program, batch 10 at 0.040 L gave the highest recovery (0.5006) but failed on fines (0.5866); batches 11 at 0.060 L and 7 at 0.080 L gave recoveries of 0.4846 and 0.4899 with fines of 0.2810 and 0.3378. Directly observed: concentrating to 0.040 L crossed the fines limit. Interpretation: excessive supersaturation caused secondary nucleation.
- Slow staged cooling was operationally associated with better particle quality. Batch 1’s short, single cooling step produced fines 0.9069 and CSD quality 0.4948, whereas batch 2’s staged cooling and aging produced fines 0.2740 and CSD quality 0.7971. This comparison is supportive, not definitive, because solvent, catalyst and seed loading also changed.
- S0/C3 was the best observed qualifying combination. Under closely similar histories, batch 7 (S0/C3) recovered 0.4899 versus 0.4572 for batch 6 (S1/C3) and 0.3638 for batch 8 (S3/C3). S1 gave better purity and fewer fines than S0, so the solvent effect was a recovery-versus-quality shift rather than universal superiority.
- Crystallization strongly purified imperfect reaction mixtures. Batch 7 had reaction selectivity 0.5112 and byproduct signal 0.3186 but crystal purity 0.9763; batch 11 had selectivity 0.5478 and purity 0.9938. The assay directly supports impurity rejection, although it does not identify the molecular mechanism.
- The tested thermal cycle did not improve the objective. Batch 12, which reheated to 290 K and recooled, gave recovery 0.4684 and fines 0.3577, versus 0.4899 and 0.3378 for the otherwise similar batch 7.

Contradicted or weakened:
- A simple monotonic rule that less solvent always creates more fines is weakened by batch 11: 0.060 L produced fewer fines than batch 7 at 0.080 L. Only the extreme 0.040 L case clearly behaved as predicted. Noise and nonlinear nucleation thresholds are plausible alternatives.
- A general benefit from extra aging was not observed. Batch 9 added two extra long terminal holds and used less seed, yet recovery (0.4859) and fines (0.3493) did not improve over batch 7. Because two factors changed, this does not separately falsify either longer aging or lower seed loading.
- The proposed ripening benefit of reheating was contradicted under the single tested cycle in batch 12. Different reheating temperatures or slower recooling remain possible.

Still untested:
- Catalyst-C3 superiority was not established causally because the catalyst comparisons also changed reaction temperature, solvent or cooling endpoint.
- The claim that batch 1’s fines arose from its 0.050 g seed loading remains untested; rapid cooling is an equally credible cause.
- No direct solubility, supersaturation, nucleation-rate or growth-rate data tested the proposed equations. The forms involving S=C/C*, J and G were interpretive organizing models.
- Replicates, a complete solvent–catalyst factorial design, seed-timing effects and the narrow solvent-volume boundary between acceptable and excessive fines were not tested.

2. One additional experiment

I would repeat batch 7 exactly but increase only the seed charge from 0.020 g to 0.050 g. This is preferable to another broad optimization because it directly separates two competing explanations for batch 1: excessive seed population versus rapid, unstaged cooling.

If seed loading is the dominant cause, the matched high-seed experiment should retain approximately similar recovery but show a distinctly smaller crystal-size index and a large increase in fines, potentially toward or beyond 0.50. If cooling history is dominant, the slow staged trajectory should keep fines near batch 7’s approximately 0.34 despite the larger seed charge, perhaps with only a modest size decrease. An intermediate result would support an interaction: slow cooling mitigates, but does not eliminate, the effect of excessive nuclei. Purity should remain high in all three cases because solvent, catalyst and reaction history would be unchanged.

3. Least-used observation and least-reliable prediction

The account used batch 3 least effectively. Its final assay showed exceptionally low fines (0.1052) and high CSD quality (0.8425), despite recovery of only 0.3792. Because both S2 and C2 differed from the principal S0/C3 series, I treated it mainly as confounded evidence. It nevertheless warns that material identity can control particle population as strongly as cooling history and that low fines need not imply high recovery.

Q09 is the least reliable held-out prediction. It filters only 60 seconds after cooling to 292 K, a regime with no campaign analogue. I predicted that the introduced seed would make particles present while seed-excluded recovery remained near zero, but the campaign did not establish how the benchmark counts seed-only solids in particle size, fines or purity immediately after seeding. Thus its particle metrics and even the operational significance of a 0.01 recovery estimate depend on an extrapolation far outside the observed residence-time range.

payload.rationale: Pairwise interpretation: Q01–Q02 isolates solvent identity; prior evidence favors S1 over S3 for recovery and purity, while both very slow ramps should suppress fines. Q03–Q04 isolates seed loading: sparse seeding should produce fewer, larger particles, with only a small kinetic recovery penalty after the exceptionally long ramp. Q05–Q06 contrasts gradual cooling with a temperature crash at equal approximate residence time; the crash should raise recovery slightly but lock in many fines. Q07–Q08 tests a terminal hold against reheating to 315 K and rapid recooling; substantial redissolution followed by fast supersaturation is expected to reduce retained recovery and regenerate fines. Q09–Q10 tests residence at 292 K: seed ensures particles are present in both, but 60 seconds gives almost no seed-excluded recovery, whereas two hours permits measurable growth. Q11–Q12 doubles reagent concentration at fixed solvent and catalyst; higher supersaturation should increase recovery but decrease size and raise fines, while remaining nominally feasible under the slow ramp. Intervals are deliberately broad because the campaign did not replicate these dilute, long-duration C1 recipes; solvent, seed, thermal-history, and concentration effects are extrapolated, and intervals near the fines threshold indicate unresolved feasibility risk.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 7 delivered the highest observed seed-excluded crystal recovery among batches meeting both constraints: crystal_yield 0.4899, crystal_purity 0.9763, and fines fraction 0.3378. Its slow staged cooling to 250 K with 0.02 g seed in solvent-S0/catalyst-C3 also provided a comfortable quality margin.
