Mechanistic account

The campaign indicates that the reaction and crystallization stages were strongly coupled through solvent identity, product concentration, impurity generation, and thermal history. All materials were anonymous benchmark identities, so the conclusions apply only to C0–C3 and S0–S3 in this fixed synthetic system.

Observed material effects

Catalyst C3 was the most useful catalyst among those carried into the later comparisons, although catalyst effects were not isolated cleanly from solvent and temperature. Batch 1 used C1/S2 at 360 K for 3600 s and reached complete conversion but gave selectivity 0.479, byproduct signal 0.359, degradation warning 0.167, and crystal recovery 0.381. Later C3 batches at 340 K for 1800 s generally had lower degradation (about 0.02–0.08) and better selectivity in favorable solvents. C0 was examined in batch 2, but under a different crystallization history; C2 was not tested. Consequently, C3 is an evidence-supported working choice, not a demonstrated global catalyst optimum.

Solvent identity affected both reaction selectivity and crystallization. Batches 7, 8, 10, and 11 form the closest solvent comparison: each used C3, 0.040 mol reagent, 0.080 L solvent, 340 K for 1800 s, quenching, 0.0001 g seed, a single 14,400 s cooling operation to 270 K, filtration, and final assay.

• Batch 7, S2: reaction yield 0.510, selectivity 0.485, crystal recovery 0.453, purity 0.977, normalized size 0.051, and fines fraction 0.987.
• Batch 8, S1: reaction yield 0.543, selectivity 0.556, crystal recovery 0.480, purity 0.974, normalized size 0.073, and fines fraction 0.987.
• Batch 10, S3: reaction yield 0.529, selectivity 0.523, crystal recovery 0.441, purity 0.961, normalized size 0.041, and fines fraction 1.000.
• Batch 11, S0: reaction yield 0.593, selectivity 0.631, crystal recovery 0.492, purity 0.987, normalized size 0.046, and fines fraction 0.994.

Thus S0 gave the largest observed reaction yield and crystallization-stage recovery, whereas S1 gave the largest particles and best CSD-quality estimate in this matched comparison. Using the instrument definition, normalized size × 250 µm, the reported d50 values were approximately 18.2 µm for batch 8, 12.8 µm for batch 7, 11.4 µm for batch 11, and 10.2 µm for batch 10. This helps explain why all four remained dominated by particles below 20 µm. The nominal dossier had suggested particularly favorable growth and low nucleation for S2, but the realized campaign favored S1 for size and S0 for recovery; fixed-world residuals or reaction-stage coupling evidently outweighed the nominal prior.

Reaction–crystallization coupling

A useful conceptual reaction scheme is parallel desired and undesired conversion:

R → P, rate rP = kP(C,S,T)·f(R)
R → I, rate rI = kI(C,S,T)·f(R)
P → D, rate rD = kD(S,T)·f(P).

Catalyst and solvent alter the relative rate constants, while excessive temperature or residence time increases byproduct and degradation exposure. Batch 1 illustrates that complete conversion alone was not sufficient: its high-temperature treatment produced poor selectivity and a strong degradation warning. In contrast, the 340 K/1800 s C3 processes preserved high conversion while improving selectivity in S0 and S1.

The crystallizer did not receive identical material merely because conversion was similar. Differences in target concentration, impurity concentration, and degradation products could change the saturation concentration, heterogeneous nucleation rate, crystal-face growth, and impurity occlusion. This is consistent with the solvent-dependent reaction and CSD results. High crystal purity throughout most of the campaign—typically about 0.96–1.00—suggests that the crystal lattice rejected impurities effectively, even when the mother liquor contained appreciable byproduct. Purity therefore ceased to be the limiting quality attribute; particle number and fines became limiting.

Crystallization interpretation

The observations are qualitatively described by supersaturation and a population balance:

S = C/C*(T,solvent),
B = kb(S−1)^b for S > 1,
G = kg(S−1)^g,
∂n(L,t)/∂t + ∂[G n(L,t)]/∂L = nucleation − dissolution ± aggregation/attrition.

Here B is the nucleation rate, G the linear growth rate, and n(L,t) the number distribution. A simple scaling for characteristic size is

d50 ∝ [Msolid/(ρN)]^(1/3),

where N is the number of crystals. Recovery can increase Msolid, but if cooling simultaneously creates a very large N through secondary nucleation, d50 remains small and the number fraction below 20 µm stays high. This appears to have occurred throughout the campaign.

Process-history dependence

Cooling history mattered, but longer or more elaborate processing was not automatically beneficial. Batch 4 used S2/C3, 0.001 g seed, and eleven successive 14,400 s cooling segments down to 270 K. It produced recovery 0.439, purity 1.000, normalized size 0.038, and fines 1.000. Batch 7 instead used 0.0001 g seed and one direct 14,400 s cool to 270 K; recovery increased to 0.453, size to 0.051, and fines decreased slightly to 0.987. Repeated cooling segments therefore did not act as a simple growth hold; they likely maintained or repeatedly regenerated nucleating supersaturation.

Batch 9 tested four additional 14,400 s holds at 270 K after the otherwise batch-8-like S1 process. Relative to batch 8, recovery changed from 0.480 to 0.471, normalized size from 0.073 to 0.023, and fines from 0.987 to 1.000. The direct observation is that the holds worsened the final CSD rather than ripening it. Secondary nucleation, attrition, or measurement variability are plausible explanations, but the campaign did not separately identify them.

Concentration also mattered. Batch 5 halved the S2 solvent volume to 0.040 L and used a small seed with staged cooling. It gave recovery 0.454 but normalized size only 0.008 and fines 1.000. The interpretation is that increased supersaturation raised the number of new nuclei faster than it raised growth per particle. This is consistent with the population-balance scaling, although concentration was confounded with the staged cooling history.

Deep cooling followed by reheating did not successfully remove fines. Batch 6 cooled gradually to 250 K and then reheated the slurry to 285 and 295 K in an attempt to dissolve small crystals selectively. Its final recovery was 0.394, purity 0.998, normalized size 0.011, and fines 1.000. In-process particle readings changed during reheating, but neither reading indicated a decisive fines reduction. The final result suggests substantial product redissolution without a sufficiently selective removal of the fine population.

Endpoint temperature showed a recovery–purity tradeoff but did not solve particle quality. Batch 12 repeated the S1-type direct process with a 275 K endpoint rather than 270 K. Compared with batch 8, recovery fell from 0.480 to 0.455 and purity increased from 0.974 to 0.988, while fines increased to 1.000. Stopping warmer therefore sacrificed recovery without creating a compliant CSD.

Recovery definitions and useful coupling metric

The reported crystal_yield is crystallization-stage recovery:

Ycryst = seed-excluded recovered target product / target product present before separation.

It is not overall yield from charged reagent. For process reasoning only, an approximate overall recovered-target fraction can be represented as

Yoverall ≈ Yreaction × Ycryst.

This gives roughly 0.26 for batch 8 (0.543 × 0.480) and 0.29 for batch 11 (0.593 × 0.492). These products are not official campaign metrics, but they show why a strong reaction solvent such as S0 could have attractive total mass productivity even though its particle quality was poor.

Revisions during the campaign

The initial approach emphasized S2 because its nominal dossier suggested low solubility, strong growth, low impurity occlusion, and low nucleation. Early batches then showed high purity and reasonable recovery but almost entirely fine particles. The campaign consequently revised seed loading downward, lengthened and staged cooling, tested aging, varied concentration, attempted temperature cycling, and finally compared all four solvents under a common direct-cooling protocol. Those revisions established that prolonged aging, extreme slow staging, concentration increase, and reheat/dissolution were not improvements in the tested forms. The solvent comparison shifted the working preference toward S1 for the best recovery/size compromise, while identifying S0 as the recovery leader.

Uncertainty and unresolved tradeoff

Final-assay standard uncertainties were approximately 0.01 for crystal recovery, 0.01 for purity, 0.025 in normalized crystal size (about 6.25 µm), and 0.018 for fines fraction. Individual size rankings are therefore uncertain, and some in-process particle measurements differed materially from final-assay size estimates. However, the fines results were approximately 0.987–1.000 in every relevant final assay, far from the required maximum of 0.50. Instrument noise cannot plausibly bridge that gap. The campaign therefore found high-purity, moderate-recovery crystallization but no quality-feasible batch.

Batch 8 remains the sealed recommendation because it combined recovery 0.480, purity 0.974, the largest observed normalized size among the matched solvent comparison, and a near-minimum fines result. This does not imply that it satisfied the fines constraint; it did not. The unresolved problem is to reduce crystal number or selectively remove fines while retaining recovery. Untested alternatives include a true controlled supersaturation feed or antisolvent addition, classification or washing that physically removes fines, different seed size distributions rather than seed mass alone, lower-shear mixing during the cooling ramp, continuous fines dissolution with external circulation, testing catalyst C2, and broader catalyst–solvent interaction designs. These mechanisms are plausible but were not demonstrated in the campaign.

1. Status of the main claims

Supported by direct observations

• Solvent identity affected both reaction and crystallization. The closest comparison was batches 7, 8, 10 and 11, which shared C3, reaction charge, heating, seed loading and direct cooling but used S2, S1, S3 and S0, respectively. Batch 11/S0 had the highest reaction yield, selectivity and crystal recovery (0.593, 0.631 and 0.492), whereas batch 8/S1 had the largest normalized crystal size and best CSD quality in that set (0.073 and 0.576). This directly supports a material effect, although the molecular explanation remains interpretive.

• Purity was not the campaign’s limiting constraint. The cited matched batches had crystal purities of 0.961–0.987, and most other completed batches were similarly high. By contrast, final fines fractions were approximately 0.987–1.000. The conclusion that particle quality, rather than purity, prevented feasibility is therefore directly supported and robust to stated assay noise.

• Additional aging did not improve the tested S1 process. Batch 9 added four 14,400 s holds after the otherwise batch-8-like crystallization. Its normalized size fell from 0.073 to 0.023 and fines rose from 0.987 to 1.000, while recovery changed from 0.480 to 0.471. The deterioration is observed; attributing it specifically to secondary nucleation or attrition is interpretation.

• Elaborate staged cooling was not automatically superior. Batch 4 used eleven slow cooling segments with S2 and gave size 0.038, recovery 0.439 and fines 1.000. Batch 7 used a much simpler direct cooling step and gave size 0.051, recovery 0.453 and fines 0.987. This supports the operational conclusion that longer schedules alone did not solve fines.

• The tested dissolution/recrystallization strategy failed. Batch 6 underwent deep cooling followed by reheating to 285 and 295 K. Its final recovery was 0.394, size 0.011 and fines 1.000. Product loss without a durable CSD improvement is directly observed. Preferential fines dissolution was the proposed mechanism, but it was contradicted in that implementation.

• A warmer final temperature traded recovery for purity without solving fines. Batch 12 ended at 275 K and gave recovery 0.455, purity 0.988 and fines 1.000, versus 0.480, 0.974 and 0.987 for batch 8 at 270 K.

Contradicted or weakened

• The nominal prior that S2 should be the best growth solvent was contradicted by the matched empirical comparison: S1 gave larger particles, while S0 gave greater recovery. The dossier was only prior evidence, so this is not an internal inconsistency; it shows that realized residuals and reaction coupling mattered.

• Simple Ostwald-ripening expectations were contradicted. Neither extended holding in batch 9 nor reheating in batch 6 produced the expected durable reduction in fines.

• The claim that higher concentration caused more secondary nucleation is plausible but weakly supported. Batch 5 used only 0.040 L S2 and ended with very small particles and fines 1.000, but it also differed in seed loading and cooling history. The observed poor CSD is real; assigning it uniquely to concentration is not justified.

Still untested

• C3 was never established as a catalyst optimum. It performed adequately in later batches, but catalyst identity was confounded with solvent and temperature. C2 was never tested, and there was no matched C0–C3 catalyst series.

• The population-balance explanation—excess secondary nucleation increasing particle number faster than crystal mass—is consistent with the results but was not directly demonstrated. No particle-number trajectory, supersaturation measurement or microscopy-based birth-rate estimate was obtained.

• The prediction that a very large seed charge combined with an extremely slow ramp could suppress fines remains essentially untested. The campaign did not run the 0.035–0.045 g seed, low-loading, multi-day schedules used in several held-out recipes. Batch 1 used 0.020 g seed, but under substantially different reaction and cooling conditions.

• The proposed overall-yield approximation, reaction yield × crystallization recovery, is bookkeeping rather than a validated kinetic law.

2. One additional experiment

I would repeat batch 4 exactly—S2/C3, 0.040 mol reagent, 0.080 L solvent, 340 K for 1800 s, quench, and the same eleven-stage slow ramp to 270 K—but increase seed mass from 0.001 g to 0.045 g. I would include non-destructive particle-size measurements after the first crystal-forming stage, midway through the ramp and immediately before filtration, followed by the normal final assay.

This changes one principal factor relative to an existing completed batch and directly tests the largest unsupported assumption in the held-out predictions.

Competing explanations and expected outcomes:

• Seeded-surface control: If campaign fines arose because insufficient seed surface allowed uncontrolled secondary nucleation, the high seed charge should consume supersaturation earlier. Fines should fall markedly, potentially toward or below 0.50, while recovery remains near batch 4’s approximately 0.44 and purity remains high. The particle trajectory should show limited creation of a new fine mode.

• Growth dilution/particle-number control: If added seed primarily increases the number of particles sharing a fixed product mass, characteristic size should decrease or remain small and fines should remain near 1.00. Recovery may change little because it is seed-excluded.

• Cooling-history control: If repeated cooling operations themselves continually generate nuclei regardless of seed surface, the high-seed experiment should still end with high fines. Intermediate measurements would show fines increasing during successive stages rather than being fixed at seeding.

A large fines reduction would support the high-seed assumptions used for Q01, Q02, Q04, Q05, Q07, Q11 and Q12. Failure would undermine the predicted feasibility of that whole group.

3. Least effectively used observation and least reliable prediction

The account used the disagreement between in-process particle measurements and final assays least effectively. For example, batch 4’s prefiltration particle measurement reported normalized size about 0.063, whereas its final assay reported about 0.038. In batch 6, successive readings changed from about 0.020 to 0.037 to 0.025, followed by a final value near 0.011. I largely treated these differences as noise. They could instead indicate real dissolution, filtration/phase-selection effects, or strong sampling variability. Without resolving that issue, mechanistic conclusions based on individual size values are less secure than conclusions based on the consistently extreme fines fractions.

Q09 is the least reliable held-out prediction. It uses a large 0.025 g seed charge, only 0.004 mol reagent, a 60 s cool to 292 K and immediate filtration. The campaign did not examine such a seed-dominated, shallow, extremely short crystallization. It is uncertain whether appreciable seed-excluded product would form, whether the recovered-solid CSD would mostly reflect the original seeds, and how purity would behave when very little new product coats them. Thus my predictions of particles being present, low but nonzero recovery, and feasible fines relied much more on extrapolation than the other estimates.

payload.rationale: The six pairs isolate: solvent (Q01–Q02), seed loading (Q03–Q04), slow ramp versus crash-cool/hold (Q05–Q06), post-ramp hold versus heat-cycle (Q07–Q08), immediate versus aged shallow crystallization (Q09–Q10), and reagent loading (Q11–Q12). I expect S1 to outperform S3 in growth, purity and recovery; a large seed charge and slow ramp to suppress secondary nucleation relative to the low-seed or crash-cooled cases; the 315 K cycle to redissolve product and create fines on rapid recooling; and aging at 292 K to raise the small seed-excluded recovery. Doubling reagent loading should raise recovery but also supersaturation, occlusion and fines. Every recipe contains an effective seed charge, so particles are expected even where seed-excluded recovery is small. Intervals are deliberately broad because campaign evidence did not directly cover this low catalyst/loading regime, final size measurements were noisy, and the predicted fines compliance of the slow-ramp and shallow-cooling cases remains uncertain.

recommendation.selection_rationale: No completed batch met the fines constraint (all final fines fractions were about 0.99-1.00). Batch 8 is the best compromise: crystal_yield 0.480, crystal_purity 0.974, and fines 0.987, with the strongest overall score among near-minimum-fines batches.

payload.report:
Mechanistic account

Observed process behavior

All batches used solvent-S2, whose public nominal profile combines relatively low solubility (0.70), low nucleation tendency (0.65), high crystal-growth tendency (1.30), and low impurity occlusion (0.65). The experiments therefore establish behavior for S2, but do not experimentally rank it against S0, S1, or S3.

Reaction performance was approximately consistent with target yield ≈ conversion × selectivity. For example, batch 1 had conversion 1.000, selectivity 0.487, and reaction yield 0.481. With catalyst-C1, the controlled-cooling batches generally retained reaction yield near 0.47 and selectivity near 0.46–0.48. The early, confounded catalyst screen gave lower final-assay selectivity with C0 (batch 2, 0.351), C2 (batch 3, 0.357), and C3 (batch 4, 0.345) than with C1 (batch 1, 0.479). This supports C1 as the best tested catalyst, although temperature, duration, and crystallization history differed across those batches, so it is not a clean catalyst-only comparison.

Crystallization strongly purified the target despite only moderate reaction selectivity. Every completed S2 batch had crystal purity above 0.97. I interpret this as preferential target incorporation and rejection of reaction byproduct from the S2 crystal phase. Thus reaction selectivity controls the amount and composition entering crystallization, while solvent-mediated solid–liquid selectivity largely controls recovered-crystal purity.

Process-history dependence was the dominant finding. Batches 1–4 were quenched before crystallization and all produced extremely high fines fractions: 0.997, 1.000, 0.995, and 1.000, respectively. Their crystal recoveries were 0.381, 0.226, 0.224, and 0.248. Batch 4 included a subsequent heat/cool cycle, but this did not repair the fines problem. My interpretation is that the abrupt quench generated a large primary-nucleation population; later aging or thermal cycling could not sufficiently eliminate that population.

In contrast, batch 5 omitted the quench and used a controlled descent from the reaction temperature to 325 K, seeding there, followed by slow cooling to 275 K. It achieved recovery 0.400, purity 0.979, and fines 0.303. This large discontinuity relative to batches 1–4 indicates that nucleation history, not merely final temperature or aging time, governed particle quality.

Within the non-quenched family, lowering the final temperature increased recovery without violating the fines constraint. With a 0.005 g seed charge, recovery rose from 0.400 at 275 K in batch 5, to 0.428 at 265 K in batch 6, and 0.450 at 250 K in batch 7. Corresponding fines fractions were 0.303, 0.294, and 0.254, while purity remained 0.979–1.000. This is consistent with a larger supersaturation/solubility driving force at lower temperature increasing deposition on an already established, limited crystal population rather than causing catastrophic secondary nucleation under the slow-cooling history.

Seeding had a smaller effect than cooling history. At 250 K, reducing seed from 0.005 g in batch 7 to 0.001 g in batch 8 slightly increased observed recovery from 0.450 to 0.455 while leaving fines essentially unchanged (0.254 in both). Omitting seed in batch 9 gave recovery 0.446 and fines 0.269. This weakly favors a small seed charge: enough to establish growth sites and control induction, but not enough to enlarge the number-weighted particle population unnecessarily. The differences are modest and should not be treated as a precisely located seed optimum.

Additional aging did not improve the result. Batch 10 repeated the 0.001 g seed/250 K strategy but used three 14,400 s holds; recovery was 0.447 and fines 0.278, versus 0.455 and 0.254 in batch 8 after one hold. This suggests that recovery was already near its practical endpoint after the standard hold, or that any slow additional growth was offset by attrition, secondary nucleation, or ordinary process variability.

Concentration introduced an unresolved recovery–quality tradeoff. Batch 11 halved S2 volume from 0.080 L to 0.040 L and used staged slow cooling. Recovery remained 0.446 and purity was 1.000, but fines rose to 0.726, violating the 0.50 limit. The likely interpretation is that higher concentration increased supersaturation enough to trigger excessive nucleation. It did not deliver a compensating recovery gain.

Useful relationships

The campaign supports the following conceptual balances:

1. Reaction target yield ≈ conversion × reaction selectivity.
2. Recovered target from the initial charge is proportional to reaction target yield × crystallization-stage recovery.
3. The reported objective recovery is specifically crystal_yield = seed-excluded recovered target product / target product present immediately before separation; it is not overall yield from the original reagent.
4. A qualitative crystallization driving force is supersaturation S = C/C*(T), with nucleation increasing steeply above a critical supersaturation while growth is favored when a limited seed population is present. The quench and concentrated batch appear to have crossed the high-nucleation regime; the gradual-cooling batches stayed mainly in a growth-dominated regime.
5. A useful product-quality constraint is to maximize crystal_yield subject to crystal_purity ≥ 0.80 and fines_number_fraction(<20 µm) ≤ 0.50. Batch 8 satisfied both with substantial margin.

Recommended-batch interpretation

Batch 8 used 0.040 mol reagent, 0.080 L S2, 0.005 mol C1, reaction heating to 355 K for 3,600 s at 300 rpm, controlled cooling to 325 K over 7,200 s, 0.001 g seed, cooling to 250 K over 14,400 s, and a 14,400 s hold at 100 rpm before filtration. Its final assay gave crystal recovery 0.4554, purity 0.9818, fines 0.2541, CSD quality 0.7946, and normalized crystal-size response 0.1178. It was the highest observed recovery among constraint-compliant batches.

Uncertainty and revisions

The strongest revision was abandoning quench-based crystallization after batches 1–4 and adopting controlled cooling before seeding. Subsequent revisions lowered terminal temperature, reduced seed dose, tested no seed and prolonged aging, and challenged the process at higher concentration.

Batch 12 repeated the batch-8 recipe and obtained recovery 0.4413, purity 0.9961, and fines 0.2690. Thus batch 8’s numerical lead is not fully separated from process and assay variability; the repeat nevertheless confirmed that the recipe robustly met both quality constraints. Differences among batches 7–10 and 12 are small relative to the reported final-assay noise and process proxy, so the evidence supports a robust operating region more strongly than an exact optimum.

Untested alternatives include other solvents, factorial catalyst comparisons at fixed conditions, intermediate solvent volumes, smaller seed-dose increments, altered seed-addition temperature, gentler multi-stage cooling rates, and controlled partial dissolution before final cooling. These could conceivably improve recovery, but the campaign provides no direct evidence that they would. The remaining practical tradeoff is that stronger supersaturation can maintain or raise recovery but may sharply increase fines, as batch 11 showed. Within the tested region, gradual cooling in 0.080 L S2 to 250 K with a small seed charge provided the best balance.

1. Support, contradiction, and remaining gaps

Supported by direct observation:
- Process history strongly tracked particle quality. Quenched batches 1–4 all had final fines fractions near unity (0.995–1.000), whereas non-quenched, gradually cooled batches 5–10 and 12 generally gave about 0.25–0.30 fines. This supports the practical claim that gradual cooling was essential. The interpretation that quenching caused excessive primary nucleation is plausible, but not yet isolated causally because the early batches also differed in catalyst, reaction conditions, seed loading, and terminal temperature.
- Lower terminal temperature improved recovery in the matched C1/S2 series: batch 5 at 275 K gave 0.400 recovery, batch 6 at 265 K gave 0.428, and batch 7 at 250 K gave 0.450. Purity remained at least 0.979 and fines remained below 0.31. This directly supports a solubility-driven recovery benefit within that tested range.
- S2 crystallization strongly purified the reaction mixture. All final crystals had purity above 0.97 even though reaction selectivity was only about 0.35–0.48. Preferential target incorporation is an interpretation; the purity observations themselves are direct.
- The concentrated batch 11 directly demonstrated a quality penalty: halving solvent volume did not improve recovery materially (0.446) but increased fines to 0.726. This supports a supersaturation–nucleation tradeoff.
- Batch 12 replicated the batch-8 operating region and again met both constraints, with recovery 0.441, purity 0.996, and fines 0.269. It supports robustness of feasibility, though not the exact superiority of batch 8.

Weakly supported or partly contradicted:
- A small seed charge appeared preferable, but the effect was weak. Batches 7, 8, and 9 gave recoveries of 0.450, 0.455, and 0.446 for 0.005 g, 0.001 g, and no seed, respectively. Those differences are comparable to assay and process uncertainty, so a precise seed optimum is not established.
- Extra aging did not produce the expected recovery or coarsening benefit: batch 10, with three long holds, gave lower recovery and higher fines than batch 8. This contradicts a simple model in which residence time alone monotonically improves growth.
- Thermal cycling did not rescue batch 4 after its quench: fines remained 1.000. That contradicts any general claim that a later heat/cool cycle necessarily erases an adverse nucleation history.
- Nominally low nucleation tendency for S2 did not prevent severe fines in batches 1–4. Thus material tendency alone was insufficient; process history dominated.
- A simple claim that higher concentration must increase fractional recovery is contradicted by batch 11, which showed little recovery benefit.

Still untested:
- No experimental comparison among S0, S1, S2, and S3 was made; all solvent rankings in the held-out predictions are extrapolations from nominal properties.
- Catalyst identity was not varied under otherwise identical conditions. The apparent C1 selectivity advantage over C0, C2, and C3 is confounded by reaction temperature, time, and downstream history.
- Primary nucleation, secondary nucleation, attrition, agglomeration, and impurity occlusion were not separately measured. Their roles remain mechanistic interpretations.
- Thermal cycling after an initially well-controlled crystallization, intermediate solvent volumes, seed-addition temperature, and detailed cooling-rate effects remain untested.

2. One additional experiment

I would run a matched quench challenge against batches 8 and 12. I would use their same charges and conditions—0.040 mol reagent, 0.080 L S2, 0.005 mol C1, 355 K for 3,600 s at 300 rpm—but insert a quench before restoring/conditioning the slurry near 325 K. I would then add 0.001 g seed, cool to 250 K over 14,400 s, hold for 14,400 s at 100 rpm, filter, and assay. An in-situ particle-size reading immediately after the quench and before seeding would be especially diagnostic.

This would distinguish two explanations: (a) quenching irreversibly creates a large nuclei population that controls the later CSD, versus (b) the poor particles in batches 1–4 arose mainly from their other recipe differences. Under explanation (a), particles or an incipient fine population should appear before seeding, final fines should rise above 0.50—potentially toward the near-unity values of batches 1–4—and size/CSD quality should decline. Recovery might rise transiently through nucleation but would not represent an acceptable quality gain. Under explanation (b), the result should remain close to batches 8 and 12: approximately 0.44–0.46 recovery, high purity, and roughly 0.25–0.27 fines. An intermediate outcome would indicate that quench history matters but interacts with final temperature, seed loading, or growth time.

3. Least-used observation and least-reliable prediction

The account used the intermediate particle-size observations least effectively. It relied mainly on final assays, despite notable differences between in-process and final readings. For example, batch 8 changed from an intermediate normalized size of 0.0748 to a final value of 0.1178, while batch 5 changed from 0.0938 to 0.0664. These differences could reflect continued evolution, filtration/sampling effects, channel noise, or representative-slurry limitations. Treating them explicitly might have better separated real growth from measurement variability and cautioned against interpreting final size and fines as a deterministic CSD pair.

Q08 is the least reliable held-out prediction. It combines several uncalibrated elements: S0 was never tested, the 0.035 g seed charge is far above the best campaign region, the preceding cooling lasts many stages, and the final 315 K dissolution/recrystallization cycle has no close campaign analogue. Batch 4 is only a weak comparator because its thermal cycle followed an already damaging quench in S2. Consequently, whether Q08’s cycle preferentially dissolves fines, dissolves most recovered product, or creates new fines during the short recool is unresolved. The sealed estimate therefore rests more on general crystallization reasoning than on direct campaign calibration.

payload.rationale: Q01–Q02: S3 is expected to outperform S1 through lower nominal solubility, nucleation and impurity occlusion, giving greater recovery, purity and size with fewer fines. Q03–Q04: increasing S0 seed loading should provide more controlled growth surface and suppress uncontrolled nucleation, moving fines below 0.50 at a modest recovery gain. Q05–Q06: the gradual 72-hour cooling profile should preserve a growth-dominated history, whereas the 120-second temperature drop should create many persistent fines even after long aging; equilibrium recovery may remain similar. Q07–Q08: the post-growth heat cycle should partially dissolve fines and improve purity/size, but some product remains dissolved or is not fully recovered during the short recool, reducing yield. Q09–Q10: a two-hour hold at 292 K permits additional deposition and growth relative to immediate filtration, but is probably insufficient to repair the fines created by the initial 60-second drop. Q11–Q12: doubling concentration should increase recovered fraction but sharply increase nucleation, impurity occlusion and fines, analogous to the campaign’s concentrated batch. All recipes contain seed, so particles are expected even where seed-excluded product recovery is small. Intervals are widest for S0, thermal cycling, high concentration and short crystallizations because these regimes were not directly calibrated; several feasibility calls near the fines threshold are consequently uncertain.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 8 gave the highest observed crystal recovery among batches meeting both constraints: crystal_yield 0.4554, crystal_purity 0.9818, and fines fraction 0.2541. Its gradual, non-quench cooling with a small seed dose avoided the severe fines seen after quenching.

payload.report:
Mechanistic account

The campaign indicates that reaction selectivity, solvent-controlled supersaturation, and crystallization history jointly determine the isolated crystals. Crystal yield here is the seed-excluded crystallization recovery, R_c = n(target in recovered crystals)/n(target present before separation); it is not overall yield from charged reagent. A useful approximate overall isolated-target fraction is therefore Y_isolated ≈ Y_reaction × R_c. For recommended batch 10, this is approximately 0.554 × 0.512 ≈ 0.284 of the initial-reagent basis, subject to the benchmark’s measurement definitions and noise.

Material effects

Solvent was the strongest observed crystallization factor. With catalyst C3 and otherwise similar 360 K reaction, seeding, cooling, aging, and filtration histories, S0 (batch 5) produced high recovery, 0.448, but an unacceptable fines fraction of 0.819. S1 (batch 6) improved recovery to 0.459 while giving 0.999 purity and acceptable fines of 0.421. S2 (batch 4) gave lower recovery, 0.377, but excellent purity and fewer fines, 0.351. S3 (batch 7) was poor on both recovery, 0.313, and fines, 0.851. Thus recovery did not follow nominal solubility alone. My interpretation is that each solvent changed reaction performance as well as product solubility, nucleation, growth, and impurity occlusion. S0 generated substantial target but excessive primary/secondary nucleation; S1 provided the best balance of target inventory, growth, and nucleation control. S2 favored clean, comparatively coarse crystallization but left more target unrecovered, while S3 combined weak reaction performance with an unfavorable particle population.

A standard supersaturation description is useful: S = C/C*(T,solvent), with nucleation J ≈ k_n(S−1)^m and growth G ≈ k_g(S−1)^g. Solvent changes C*, k_n, k_g, and impurity incorporation. Seeded, gradual cooling should direct supersaturation toward growth rather than uncontrolled nucleation. The solvent results are consistent with this framework, but the individual kinetic constants were not measured.

Catalyst C3 was retained after the early screen. The closest comparison was batch 1 versus batch 4: both used S2, 360 K for one hour, 0.02 g seed, cooling to 280 K, and an aging period. C3 in batch 4 gave recovery 0.377 and fines 0.351, versus 0.347 and 0.384 with C1 in batch 1. The final reaction yields were similar, about 0.431 versus 0.428, although degradation was higher with C3. C0 in batch 2 and C2 in batch 3 were less attractive, but those comparisons were confounded by different reaction temperatures, seed charges, and cooling histories. Therefore C3 is the best observed choice, not a cleanly isolated catalyst optimum.

Reaction–crystallization coupling

Conversion was generally near unity, so product formation was governed mainly by selectivity and degradation rather than residual reactant. Final reaction selectivity varied substantially across solvent–catalyst combinations: approximately 0.375 in batch 2, 0.573 in batch 5, 0.520 in batch 6, and 0.360 in batch 7. Nevertheless, crystal purity remained 0.967–1.000. This shows that crystallization was highly selective and rejected much of the reaction byproduct even when liquid-phase selectivity was only moderate.

The reaction was not quenched before crystallization. Consequently, catalyst-mediated reaction or degradation could continue during cooling and aging, and HPLC immediately after heating was not always identical to the final assay. For example, batch 4 had post-heating HPLC yield/selectivity of 0.477/0.465 but final values of 0.431/0.445. This may reflect continued chemistry, phase redistribution, sampling differences, and instrument noise. A quenched versus unquenched comparison was not performed, so continued reaction during crystallization remains an interpretation rather than a proven mechanism.

Process-history dependence and revisions

The initial strategy favored S2 because its nominal dossier suggested low solubility, strong growth, and low impurity occlusion. Batches 1–4 screened catalysts and cooling/seed histories in S2. After C3 performed best in the closest comparison, batches 5–7 screened solvents. S1 emerged as the best feasible solvent and was then optimized in batches 8–12 by lowering the crystallization endpoint and changing seed/cooling history.

With S1/C3, 0.02 g seed, four-hour cooling, and four-hour aging, reducing the endpoint from 280 K to 270, 260, and 250 K increased observed recovery from 0.459 in batch 6 to 0.492, 0.498, and 0.512 in batches 8, 9, and 10. At the same time, fines moved from 0.395 at 270 K to 0.424 at 260 K and 0.457 at 250 K. This is the central recovery–quality tradeoff: deeper cooling increased thermodynamic recovery but also increased nucleation and approached the fines limit.

Increasing seed from 0.02 g in batch 10 to 0.05 g in batch 11 reduced the recovery point estimate from 0.512 to 0.503, while improving purity from 0.978 to 0.993 and fines from 0.457 to 0.443. These differences are modest relative to assay uncertainty, but they are consistent with additional seed surface moderating supersaturation and fines at a small apparent recovery cost.

Batch 12 used staged cooling, first to 280 K and then to 250 K, followed by aging. Its in-process particle measurements showed fines decreasing from 0.406 after the first cooling stage to 0.362 after the second and 0.352 after aging, while normalized crystal size increased from 0.060 to 0.073 and then 0.116. The final assay gave recovery 0.504, purity 0.994, fines 0.362, and size 0.104. Thus staged cooling and aging produced a much more robust particle-quality margin than direct cooling in batch 10, but did not exceed batch 10’s recovery point estimate.

Recommendation and uncertainty

The sealed recommendation remains batch 10 because it had the highest observed feasible seed-excluded recovery: 0.512, with purity 0.978 and fines 0.457. Purity is comfortably above 0.80, but the fines margin is only 0.043. Final-assay standard deviations were approximately 0.010 for crystal yield, 0.010 for purity, 0.018 for fines, and 0.025 for normalized size. The 0.007 recovery difference between batches 10 and 12 is therefore not statistically resolved by single measurements. Batch 12 may be the more robust quality process, whereas batch 10 remains the correct choice under the stated objective of maximizing the observed recovery subject to the measured constraints.

Important untested alternatives include replicated batches 10 and 12; a quenched reaction before crystallization; finer multistage or continuous cooling ramps; lower stirring during supersaturation generation; seed-size and seed-timing studies; filtration at controlled low temperature; and a fully matched catalyst/temperature/duration factorial. These could determine whether batch 10’s recovery advantage is reproducible and whether staged cooling can retain its lower fines while matching or exceeding the recovery of direct 250 K cooling.

1. Status of the main claims

Supported by direct observations:
- Solvent strongly affected recovery and particle quality. Under closely related C3 conditions, batch 5 (S0) gave crystal yield 0.448 but fines 0.819; batch 6 (S1) gave 0.459 yield with fines 0.421; batch 7 (S3) gave only 0.313 yield with fines 0.851. S1 therefore provided the best feasible balance in that comparison. The explanation in terms of solvent-dependent solubility, nucleation, growth, and occlusion remains an interpretation; those kinetic quantities were not measured separately.
- Deeper direct cooling in S1 increased recovery while narrowing the fines margin. Batches 8, 9, and 10 ended at 270, 260, and 250 K and gave yields of 0.492, 0.498, and 0.512, while fines rose from 0.395 to 0.424 and 0.457. This directly supports a recovery–quality tradeoff for that process family.
- Staging and aging changed the particle distribution. In batch 12, particle measurements progressed from size/fines 0.060/0.406 after the 280 K stage to 0.073/0.362 after 250 K and 0.116/0.352 after aging. Its final assay, 0.104/0.362, confirmed a substantially better fines margin than batch 10, although recovery was slightly lower at 0.504 versus 0.512.
- Crystallization was selective. Even when final reaction selectivity was only about 0.36–0.57, crystal purity was 0.967–1.000 across the solvent screen. That directly supports impurity rejection during crystallization.

Supported only weakly or with confounding:
- C3 appeared better than C1 in the closest comparison: batch 4 versus batch 1 gave recovery 0.377 versus 0.347 and fines 0.351 versus 0.384. However, single-batch noise and subtle history differences prevent a strong catalyst ranking. C0 and C2 were tested with different temperatures, seed loads, and cooling histories, so their apparent inferiority is not a clean catalyst effect.
- Raising seed from 0.02 g in batch 10 to 0.05 g in batch 11 improved purity and fines but reduced the recovery estimate from 0.512 to 0.503. Those changes are comparable to assay uncertainty, so the proposed supersaturation-buffering effect of additional seed is plausible rather than established.

Contradicted or revised:
- The initial expectation that S2’s nominal low solubility, strong growth, and low occlusion would make it optimal was contradicted for the stated recovery objective. S2 produced clean particles in batch 4, but S1 subsequently delivered higher feasible recovery in batches 6 and 8–10.
- A simple claim that lower temperature intrinsically creates more fines is incomplete. The matched endpoint series in batches 8–10 showed that trend, but the within-batch measurements in staged batch 12 showed fines falling as cooling and aging proceeded. Cooling rate and history therefore modify, and can overcome, the endpoint-temperature effect.
- Solubility alone cannot explain the solvent ranking. S0 gave relatively high recovery in batch 5 despite its nominally higher solubility, while also giving extreme fines. Its stronger reaction yield and resulting target concentration probably contributed to supersaturation, but that causal link was not isolated.

Still untested:
- Continued reaction or degradation during crystallization remains unproven because no campaign batch included an otherwise matched quench/no-quench comparison.
- The suggested nucleation and growth relationships, J≈k_n(S−1)^m and G≈k_g(S−1)^g, are organizing models rather than fitted laws.
- Whether batch 10 truly has higher recovery than batch 12 is unresolved: their 0.007 difference is smaller than the approximate single-assay crystal-yield standard deviation of 0.010.
- Effects of seed size distribution, filtration temperature, washing, continuous ramp shape, and matched catalyst-dose or reaction-time changes were not tested.

2. One additional experiment

I would repeat the batch-10 S1/C3 recipe with one deliberate change: take an HPLC measurement immediately after the 360 K reaction, then quench before seeding, cool directly to 250 K over four hours, age for four hours, filter, terminate, and perform the final assay. The reagent, solvent, catalyst, seed, stirring, cooling, aging, and filtration conditions would otherwise match batch 10.

This would distinguish two explanations for the differences between post-heating HPLC and final reaction metrics:
- If catalyst-mediated reaction or degradation continued during the unquenched crystallization, the quenched experiment should preserve its post-reaction yield/selectivity. Its final byproduct and degradation signals should differ from batch 10, and altered target/impurity concentrations could change crystal recovery or purity.
- If those discrepancies arose mainly from instrument noise, phase redistribution, or sampling, quenching should leave the final reaction and crystal outcomes close to batch 10 within uncertainty.

A particularly informative outcome would be unchanged crystal recovery but improved purity after quenching, indicating that continued chemistry mainly generated impurities. Lower recovery after quenching would imply that useful product formation continued during batch 10’s cooling/aging period. Higher recovery with lower degradation would instead indicate that the unquenched catalyst primarily destroyed target during that period.

3. Least effectively used observation and least reliable prediction

The account used batch 5 least effectively. Its combination of the highest reaction yield in the solvent screen, about 0.567, relatively high crystal recovery, 0.448, and extremely poor fines, 0.819, contains evidence that reaction-generated target concentration and crystallization supersaturation were coupled. I mainly described it as an intrinsic S0 nucleation problem. A better treatment would have separated the solvent’s direct nucleation tendency from its indirect effect through reaction yield and target concentration. The campaign did not provide the matched data needed to quantify those contributions.

Q08 is the least reliable held-out prediction. It reheats an established crystal population to 315 K and then allows only one hour of recooling. No campaign batch tested partial dissolution, seed survival, polymorph/history reset, or recrystallization after such a thermal cycle. Consequently, my sealed estimates for its surviving particles, recovery, size improvement, and reduced fines depend on an unverified assumption that heating preferentially dissolves fines without fully erasing the crystal population. Complete dissolution followed by insufficient renucleation, or rapid secondary nucleation during recooling, could produce qualitatively different outcomes.

payload.rationale: The six pairs isolate solvent (Q01–Q02), seed loading (Q03–Q04), gradual versus crash cooling (Q05–Q06), low-temperature aging versus a heat–recool cycle (Q07–Q08), immediate filtration versus a 2 h hold (Q09–Q10), and reagent concentration (Q11–Q12). I expect S1 to give higher recovery and fewer fines than S3; heavy seeding to suppress primary nucleation relative to the very low-seed case; and gradual cooling to produce larger particles and fewer fines than a rapid initial temperature drop, with similar long-time recovery. The heat cycle should dissolve fines and improve size distribution and purity, but its short recooling period may not restore all dissolved product. At 292 K, seeds ensure particles are present, but immediate filtration should recover almost no seed-excluded product; the hold permits limited growth. Doubling reagent concentration should substantially increase supersaturation and recovery, while increasing impurity occlusion and secondary nucleation. Intervals are deliberately broad because these recipes use much lower catalyst concentration, smaller volume, quenching, and far longer cooling histories than the campaign; uncertainty is greatest for thermal cycling, near-zero recovery, and the concentration extrapolation.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 10 gave the highest observed seed-excluded crystal recovery (0.512) while meeting crystal purity (0.978 >= 0.80) and fines (0.457 <= 0.50) constraints.

payload.report:
Mechanistic account

Recommended process and outcome
Batch 8 remains the recommendation: 0.040 mol reagent, 0.080 L solvent-S2, 0.005 mol catalyst-C1, reaction at 330 K for 1,800 s with 500 rpm stirring, addition of 0.050 g seed, cooling to 255 K over 14,400 s, immediate filtration, termination, and final assay. Its observed seed-excluded crystal recovery was 0.4176, with crystal purity 0.9800 and fines number fraction 0.4741. Thus it gave the highest observed recovery among batches satisfying purity >=0.80 and fines <=0.50.

Material effects and reaction–crystallization coupling
Solvent-S2 was selected from the supplied prior because it had the lowest nominal relative solubility (0.70), highest relative crystal growth (1.30), lowest nucleation tendency (0.65), and lowest impurity occlusion (0.65). Consistent with that prior, every assayed S2 process produced very pure crystals (approximately 0.976–1.000). However, no other solvent was experimentally tested, so superiority over S0, S1, or S3 remains an interpretation rather than a demonstrated ranking.

Catalyst identity strongly affected downstream particle quality even when the nominal crystallization procedure was similar. With C0, batches 2, 4, 5, and 6 gave recoveries of 0.414–0.428 but fines fractions of 0.681–0.694. With C1 at full solvent volume, batches 7–9 and 12 gave fines of 0.472, 0.474, 0.491, and 0.489 while retaining recoveries of 0.404–0.418. This is the clearest observed reaction–crystallization coupling.

The coupling is not explained simply by bulk crystal purity: both catalyst families produced approximately 0.98–1.00 purity. C0 often showed somewhat better liquid-phase reaction selectivity (roughly 0.49–0.52 in batches 2 and 4–6) than C1 (roughly 0.45–0.48 in batches 7–9 and 12), yet its particle distribution was much worse. A plausible interpretation is that catalyst-dependent residual species, byproduct identity, or solution speciation changed heterogeneous nucleation or crystal-growth kinetics without being captured by the scalar purity measurement. Catalyst carryover acting as nucleation sites is another possibility. These alternatives were not independently assayed and therefore remain unresolved.

Reaction severity mattered. Batch 1 used C1 but was heated at 350 K for 3,600 s; it showed byproduct signal 0.382 and degradation warning 0.154, versus degradation warnings near 0.04–0.06 for the 330 K, 1,800 s C1 processes. Its reaction selectivity was only 0.441. The revised 330 K/1,800 s condition therefore reduced apparent degradation while maintaining essentially complete conversion. For example, batch 8 gave conversion 1.000, reaction selectivity 0.480, and liquid-product yield 0.468. The evidence supports avoiding the hotter, longer reaction, although reaction temperature and residence time were not mapped independently.

Crystallization mechanism and concentration effects
A useful qualitative description is supersaturation-controlled competition between nucleation and growth:

S = (C - C*)/C*,
B = k_b S^b,
G = k_g S^g,

where S is supersaturation, B is nucleation rate, and G is crystal-growth rate. Conditions that make B large relative to G create many small particles and raise the number fraction below 20 micrometres. Recovery can be approximated by

R_cryst = n_target,recovered excluding seed / n_target,before separation,

and, at equilibrium, tends to increase as the residual dissolved amount C*(T_f)V decreases. This recovery is explicitly a crystallization-stage recovery, not overall yield from charged reagent. If reaction and crystallization definitions are treated as approximately compatible, batch 8’s overall recovered-target fraction would be on the order of reaction yield times crystallization recovery, about 0.47 × 0.42, rather than 0.42 of the initial reagent.

The solvent-volume study supports a nonlinear supersaturation effect. At 0.080 L, C1 batches 7–9 and 12 all met the fines constraint. Reducing S2 to 0.060 L in batch 10 still worked (recovery 0.4064, fines 0.4716, purity 0.9811). Reducing it further to 0.040 L in batch 11 caused a sharp fines increase to 0.9934, despite recovery of 0.4129 and purity of 0.9995. The most likely interpretation is that the concentrated charge crossed a nucleation threshold, creating an overwhelming number of fine particles. This sharp response argues against pursuing recovery by concentration alone.

Temperature revealed a narrower tradeoff under the preferred C1/full-volume conditions. Direct cooling gave:
- Batch 7, 260 K: recovery 0.4064, fines 0.4716.
- Batch 8, 255 K: recovery 0.4176, fines 0.4741.
- Batch 9, 250 K: recovery 0.4138, fines 0.4910.
- Batch 12, 255 K replicate: recovery 0.4035, fines 0.4891.

The expected thermodynamic tendency is increased recovery at lower temperature, but the observed recovery differences are small relative to process and assay variability. Fines generally approached the constraint at the coldest settings. Consequently, 255 K represents an empirical compromise rather than proof of a sharply defined optimum.

Process-history dependence
Batch 1 cooled to 280 K and was then held for 7,200 s; during the hold the vessel warmed toward ambient before filtration. It produced particularly low fines (0.3605) but only 0.3317 recovery. This is consistent with partial dissolution or Ostwald-type ripening removing the smallest crystals at the cost of recovered mass. Because batch 1 also used the harsher reaction, the thermal-history contribution cannot be isolated.

Batch 3 deliberately used a cycle of cooling to 250 K, reheating to 285 K, and recooling to 260 K. It met the constraints (recovery 0.3721, purity 0.9897, fines 0.4859), but recovery was lower than in the simpler direct-cooling C1 batches 7–9. The cycle may have dissolved fines and allowed regrowth, but it offered no recovery advantage. With C0, a more extensive 250→290→255 K cycle in batch 4 failed to correct the fines problem (0.6940), showing that thermal annealing could not overcome the catalyst-associated CSD effect under the tested conditions. Similarly, warming after cold crystallization in C0 batch 5 still left fines at 0.6876. These observations motivated the revision toward simple, direct cooling with C1.

Revisions during the campaign
The work progressed from a hotter reaction and warm crystallization in batch 1, through deeper cooling with C0 in batch 2, thermal cycling in batches 3–5, and direct-temperature tests in batches 6–9. The large catalyst-dependent fines contrast shifted emphasis from maximizing nominal reaction selectivity to controlling downstream nucleation. Batches 10–11 then tested concentration, revealing the severe fines penalty at 0.040 L. Batch 12 repeated the chosen batch-8 recipe and confirmed feasibility, though with modestly lower recovery.

Uncertainty and unresolved tradeoff
Batch 8 and its batch-12 replicate gave recoveries of 0.4176 and 0.4035, purities of 0.9800 and 0.9944, and fines of 0.4741 and 0.4891. Their mean recovery is about 0.411 and their mean fines fraction about 0.482. This reproducibility supports the process region, but both fines results lie close to the 0.50 constraint. The final-assay fines noise specification was approximately 0.018, and independent in-process particle measurements also placed several batches near the boundary (batch 8: 0.4862; batch 9: 0.5006; batch 12: 0.4911). Therefore the recommendation qualifies on observed final assays but has limited fines margin.

The unresolved optimization problem is a recovery–robustness tradeoff. Deeper cooling or greater concentration might increase thermodynamic recovery, but the tested evidence shows increasing or catastrophic fines risk. Warmer holds or thermal cycling can lower fines in some histories, but they sacrifice recovery and were not consistently effective. A future study could test slightly warmer final temperatures, controlled cooling-rate profiles, seed-size distributions, or a modestly larger solvent volume to create more fines margin; none of those alternatives was tested here. Catalyst carryover and solution speciation should also be measured directly to determine why C1 controls fines much better than C0.

1. Status of the main claims

Supported by direct observations:
- Catalyst choice was strongly associated with downstream fines. C0 batches 2, 4, 5, and 6 had final fines fractions of about 0.681–0.694, whereas full-volume C1 batches 7, 8, 9, and 12 gave 0.472–0.491. This association is robust within the campaign.
- Batch 8’s operating region was reproducible but close to the fines boundary. Batch 8 gave recovery 0.4176, purity 0.9800, and fines 0.4741; its recipe replicate, batch 12, gave 0.4035, 0.9944, and 0.4891.
- Purity was not the binding constraint. All completed batches had very high assayed crystal purity, approximately 0.976–1.000, including the high-fines C0 batches.
- A severe concentration effect was observed. Reducing S2 from 0.080 L to 0.060 L in batch 10 retained acceptable fines (0.4716), but 0.040 L in batch 11 produced fines of 0.9934. Calling this a nucleation threshold is an interpretation, but the abrupt empirical deterioration is direct evidence.
- The hotter, longer reaction in batch 1 showed more degradation and byproduct signal: degradation warning 0.154 and byproduct signal 0.382, versus warnings around 0.04–0.06 for the later 330 K/1,800 s C1 batches. Avoiding that harsher reaction is therefore supported, although temperature and duration were changed together.

Supported only as interpretations:
- Catalyst carryover acting as heterogeneous nucleation sites is plausible, but catalyst identity was never separated from catalyst-dependent reaction composition or solution speciation. The observation supports coupling, not that particular mechanism.
- The account attributed batch 11’s fines excursion to high supersaturation and nucleation. That is consistent with the volume series, but volume, concentration, and solvent-to-solute ratio were not independently varied.
- The low fines and low recovery in batch 1 are consistent with dissolution/ripening during its warm post-cooling history, but its harsher reaction is a confounder.

Contradicted or weakened:
- Recovery did not increase monotonically with deeper final cooling. For otherwise similar C1 batches, recovery was 0.4064 at 260 K (batch 7), 0.4176 at 255 K (batch 8), and 0.4138 at 250 K (batch 9). Any thermodynamic trend was smaller than process variation over this range.
- Thermal annealing was not a generally effective fines remedy. Batch 3’s cycle qualified but recovered only 0.3721, while direct-cooling batches 7–9 recovered about 0.406–0.418. C0 batch 4 remained at 0.694 fines after cycling, and warming after cooling did not rescue batch 5.
- Greater concentration did not demonstrably improve recovery: batches 10 and 11 recovered 0.4064 and 0.4129, neither exceeding batch 8, while batch 11 suffered a major CSD penalty.
- A simple “more bulk impurity causes more fines” explanation is weakened because C0 often had better scalar reaction selectivity than C1 yet much worse fines, while final crystal purity remained high.

Still untested:
- The claimed superiority of S2 over S0, S1, and S3. Every campaign batch used S2; its favorable nominal dossier was prior evidence, not an experimental solvent comparison.
- Whether C0 itself, a C0-derived product/byproduct, or another unmeasured solution property causes the fines increase.
- Effects of seed size distribution, cooling rate independent of final temperature, catalyst removal, washing, and solvent mixtures.
- Robust operation with a comfortable fines margin below 0.50; the recommended region was feasible but marginal.

2. One additional experiment

I would run a catalyst-loading discrimination experiment using 0.040 mol reagent, 0.080 L S2, and only 0.0005 mol C0. I would react at 330 K, using a longer residence time if needed to approach the conversion of batch 8, take an HPLC measurement before crystallization, then add 0.050 g seed, cool directly to 255 K over 14,400 s, measure particle size, filter, terminate, and assay.

This single batch would be compared with the high-C0-loading batches 2/4–6 and the C1 reference batches 8/12. It would distinguish three explanations:
- If C0 acts mainly through catalyst-particle or catalyst-concentration-dependent heterogeneous nucleation, a tenfold reduction should move fines from about 0.69 toward the C1 range near 0.47–0.49 while retaining reasonable recovery.
- If catalyst identity creates a potent dissolved nucleation promoter even at low loading, fines should remain high despite the reduced C0 amount.
- If the effect is mediated mainly by reaction composition, fines should track the measured HPLC byproduct/selectivity profile rather than catalyst loading itself. A C1-like chromatographic profile with C0-like fines would argue against the scalar reaction-composition explanation; simultaneous improvement of both would support it.

The cleanest favorable result would be purity above 0.95, recovery around 0.40, and fines below 0.50. Persisting fines near 0.65–0.70 would strongly support an identity-specific C0 effect. An intermediate result would indicate a dose-dependent coupling and motivate a proper catalyst-loading series.

3. Least effectively used observation and least reliable prediction

The account used crystal_size least effectively. It focused on recovery, purity, and the thresholded fines fraction, but the observed median-size metric was not redundant with fines. For example, batch 2 had crystal_size 0.1027 despite fines 0.681, while batch 1 had size 0.0786 and much lower fines of 0.360. Batch 8 had size 0.1076 and fines 0.474, whereas batch 12 had size 0.0989 and fines 0.489. These combinations suggest broad or possibly bimodal distributions: a respectable d50 can coexist with a large sub-20 µm population. Treating “larger size” and “fewer fines” as one mechanism therefore lost information.

Q02 is the least reliable held-out prediction. Its optimistic S3 estimates rely almost entirely on nominal solvent properties—lower solubility and occlusion and better growth/nucleation balance—because the campaign supplied no experimental evidence for S3 or any solvent other than S2. It also extrapolates to a much smaller charge, a hotter quenched reaction, and an exceptionally long multistage cooling history. Hidden solvent-specific residuals could reverse the nominal ranking. Q01 has the same general limitation for S1, but Q02 made the stronger favorable extrapolation and is therefore the most vulnerable sealed prediction.

payload.rationale: Q01–Q02: S3 is predicted to outperform S1 because its lower nominal solubility and impurity occlusion, lower nucleation tendency, and higher growth tendency should raise recovery, purity, and size while reducing fines. Q03–Q04: greater seeding should suppress uncontrolled primary nucleation and modestly improve recovery and CSD, although seed-excluded yield does not count the seed itself. Q05–Q06: the gradual ramp and cold shock have similar final temperature and total time, so equilibrium recovery is similar, but the shock is expected to generate substantially more fines. Q07–Q08: the 315 K excursion should redissolve product; only one hour of recooling is unlikely to restore recovery and may cause renewed nucleation, despite some purification. Q09–Q10: seed particles remain present in both, but 60 seconds gives almost no seed-excluded deposition; the two-hour hold increases recovery and growth but probably remains fines-limited. Q11–Q12: doubling reagent concentration should increase recovered fraction but cross toward a high-nucleation regime, reducing size and worsening fines and occlusion. Intervals are deliberately broad because the recipes extrapolate far beyond the campaign in solvent identity, concentration, cooling duration, and thermal history; feasibility is assigned from the point estimates, not guaranteed by the intervals.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Highest observed seed-excluded crystal recovery among completed batches meeting both quality constraints: crystal_yield 0.4176, crystal_purity 0.9800, and fines fraction 0.4741. The full-solvent, C1-catalyzed, seeded slow-cooling process also showed reproducible feasibility in nearby batches.
